# Evaluation Engineering — Complete Text

> A working wiki on evaluation engineering: the discipline of designing, building, and operating systems that produce large numbers of estimates and evaluations at known cost. Maintained by QURI as part of the CAIRN project.
>
> This is the entire wiki concatenated into one document, in book reading order,
> for offline reading (e-readers) and LLM context. Web version: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org



================================================================================
# Start Here
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## 1. Evaluation Engineering
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/start-here/introduction/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, revised October 2026. This page states a framing, not a settled position.*

## The one-sentence version

**Evaluation engineering is the design of systems that produce large numbers of estimates and evaluations at known cost, under incentives that keep them honest.**

We know how to produce one careful evaluation: hire a capable person, give them time, read the report. We are bad at producing the ten-thousandth as cheaply and reliably as the first, keeping all ten thousand consistent as the world changes, and keeping the system trusted once the evaluated start to care about the scores.

## What problem this responds to

Prediction markets, forecasting tournaments and proposals like futarchy looked promising two decades ago. Markets have since become a large business, mostly sports betting, but they and tournaments remain rare as inputs to decisions in government, firms, or even the communities that champion them. One diagnosis is that prediction was never the whole product. Getting from "we can forecast this clean, verifiable question" to "we can put a defensible number on what the decision turns on" needs a structured set of questions (ontology), calculation that chains inputs into derived estimates, prediction to keep the system calibrated, and evaluation to resolve questions with no clean ground truth ([The Four Components](/concepts/components/)). Whole machines exist where budgets are large and questions stable: credit scoring, health technology assessment, GiveWell's cost-effectiveness models. For most grants, organizations, research claims and policies, nobody was building one.

## Why "engineering", and what it has to include

The framing borrows from systems disciplines (lean manufacturing, software architecture) rather than from the philosophy of value or from program evaluation, whose centre of gravity is the individual study ([Adjacent Fields §3](/reference/adjacent-fields/)). The questions are throughput, cost per item, consistency, failure modes, and how a change to one estimate propagates to the estimates that depend on it. At scale, optimizing any single evaluation is usually the wrong objective.

Certification economics complicates this: who pays a certifier shapes what it certifies ([Patterns §3](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#3-incentives-and-funding-shape-trustworthiness)). When the [catalogue](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/#does-who-pays-predict-failure) was coded, neither payer type nor method predicted documented failure, but systems paid by the parties they rate had about 3.5 times the odds of one, mostly through gaming by the rated party. The coding is weak evidence (one coder, documented failures only), but a purely technical programme would not have looked. This wiki therefore treats payer, metric ownership, disclosure and appeal as design variables alongside staffing and data, and treats robustness to gaming and legitimacy as properties a design must deliver alongside accuracy and cost ([Evaluation as a System](/concepts/the-systems-view/#the-design-space)). Mechanism design is part of the engineering.

## The core split: estimation vs. evaluation

**Estimation** is producing numbers a careful analyst could check: Fermi estimates, models, sums. **Evaluation** is judgment on messy questions, where the result is useful only if its audience trusts it ("how much did this organization reduce existential risk?"). The design heuristic is divide and conquer: push as much as possible into cheap, verifiable estimation, and confine judgment-bound evaluation to a smaller, more expensive layer. See [Estimation vs. Evaluation](/start-here/estimation-vs-evaluation/).

## The core pattern

The technique this wiki leans on most is the [prediction–evaluation system](/concepts/techniques/#predictionevaluation-systems): a cheap layer (forecasters, a statistical model, now an LLM) predicts what an expensive, trusted evaluator would conclude on every item; a hidden random subset is sent to the expensive evaluator; the cheap layer's agreement on that subset is measured against how often two expensive evaluators agree with each other. QURI's founder wrote this up in 2018, but it was not new. Psychologists showed by 1970 that a statistical model of an expert judge can out-predict the judge, automated essay scoring has run the pattern for years, DARPA's SCORE program ran it on social-science replication, and prediction-powered inference supplies its statistics ([Lineage](/start-here/lineage/#outside-precedents-for-the-core-pattern)).

## Why evaluation, specifically?

The founding draft's slogan is that highly optimized evaluations are "(almost) all you need". Two claims sit behind it:

- **Evaluation may be most of the valuable output.** Many high-stakes processes are evaluation problems: courts, grantmaking, hiring, impact assessment, policy choice. It is plausible that more resources flow into evaluation than into clean estimation. Nobody has measured this.
- **The accuracy bar is lower than it looks.** Outputs need only beat what people would otherwise have done, cheaply enough to be used. People already make vast numbers of noisy informal judgments ([Objections](/reference/objections/)).

The slogan is the least-supported claim in the wiki and nothing else depends on it.

## Not AI model evals, though they overlap

In current AI usage, "evals" means test suites and judges that measure AI models and AI products: capability and safety evaluations by groups such as [METR](https://metr.org/), whose time-horizon metric tracks the length of tasks models can complete ([Kwa et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499)); open frameworks such as the UK AI Security Institute's [Inspect](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/); and rubric-based testing of LLM applications. That field is large and well funded. This wiki uses "evaluation" in the older sense of judging grants, organizations, policies and research, where an AI is a possible *evaluator* rather than the thing evaluated.

The two meet wherever an LLM is the judge. Validating a judge against humans, putting error bars on results ([Miller 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640)), and watching a leaderboard get gamed (selective disclosure of privately tested model variants biased Chatbot Arena scores; [Singh et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879)) are shared problems, and the [LLM chapter](/concepts/llm-evaluators/) and [Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/) draw on the AI-evals literature for them. Whether the name should change is [crux 12](/start-here/key-questions/#on-the-field-itself).

## Why this might be worth a field

- **Generality.** Better evaluation systems would help impact assessment, policy, research prioritization and grantmaking at once.
- **Neglect, partly.** The components (forecasting, decision analysis, survey methodology, LLM judging) are each studied. Their integration into audited, high-throughput systems for judging grants, organizations and policies is not, as far as this wiki can tell. The AI-evals boom weakens this claim for anything that looks like judging model outputs.
- **Timing.** LLMs make the labor-intensive steps (drafting evaluations, structuring questions, running calculations) cheap. Whether they make them trustworthy is the open question ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/)).

## What this wiki is not yet

It does not commit to a software stack, an institutional form, or claims about cost-effectiveness; those depend on experiments not yet run. Its [capability ladder](/concepts/capability-ladder/) is a v0 graded on eight systems, and its one fully priced design is the fictional [worked example](/concepts/worked-example/).


------------------------------------------------------------
## 2. Estimation vs. Evaluation
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/start-here/estimation-vs-evaluation/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: early draft, adapted from the 2021–22 estimation-theory notes (see [Lineage](/start-here/lineage/)).*

## Estimation

**Estimation** is the calculation of specific numbers, usually under uncertainty. It is a superset of ordinary numeric calculation: summing itemized expenses is "estimation" with no uncertainty; a Fermi estimate is "estimation" with a lot.

The defining property: the estimator only has to be *correct*, and correctness can in principle be checked. In practice estimates carry contestable modelling choices (which inputs, which structure, which discount rate), so "only has to be correct" is an idealization; the point is that disagreements are about facts and models rather than about what is good.

Examples:

- How many piano tuners are in Boston right now?
- How many total hours have been spent reading a particular blog post?
- How much do Americans spend on mechanical keyboards per year?

Estimation leans on logic, math, economics, and data engineering.

## Evaluation

**Evaluation** is similar — it also produces a judgment, often numeric — but for things that are *messy*: results that are difficult or impossible to verify or fully trust. Evaluations either avoid formal models or use them as one input among many (à la [cluster thinking](https://blog.givewell.org/2014/06/10/sequence-thinking-vs-cluster-thinking/)).

The defining property: here the *effect on the audience matters*. The number usually needs explanation, the explanation needs to be tailored to readers, and — crucially — the result is only useful if the relevant people *trust* it. An excellent evaluation nobody believes changes nothing.

Examples:

- On a scale of 0–100, how good a job did Barack Obama do as president?
- What is the probability that we live in a simulation?
- How much did organization X reduce existential risk from 2000 to 2020?

Evaluation leans on psychometrics, survey methodology, sociology and epistemology.

Program evaluation draws the line differently, and more sharply. Scriven defines evaluation as determining the "merit, worth, or significance" of something, which requires value premises (criteria and standards) as well as facts ([Key Evaluation Checklist](https://files.wmich.edu/s3fs-public/attachments/u1105/2023/kec-scriven.pdf)). On that definition the simulation question above is a hard *estimate*, not an evaluation. This wiki's split is mainly about verifiability and trust, and the two criteria usually coincide: the questions hardest to verify are usually the ones that embed contested values.

## The distinction is a gradient, not a wall

There is no crisp line. Many real questions sit in between. A rough contrast:

| Estimation | Evaluation |
|---|---|
| Highly quantitative | Highly qualitative |
| Relies on equations/models | Relies on judgment and intuition |
| Easy for parties to agree on | Parties hold different underlying intuitions |
| Little trust in the estimator needed | Lots of trust in the evaluator needed |
| Terminology rarely contested | Terminology frequently contested |
| Minimal explanation | Often substantial explanation |
| Usually numeric | Numeric, grades, scales, or prose |
| Math, programming, data, economics | Economics, sociology, epistemology, mixed methods |

A useful intuition pump: which questions would you hand to *a sharp quantitative analyst* (estimation), and which would you want *a team of trusted domain experts or strong generalists* on (evaluation)?

## Why separate them: divide and conquer

The payoff of the distinction is a design strategy, borrowed from the functional-programming idea of separating pure from impure code:

> Handle as much as possible as **estimation**. Sequester the genuinely judgment-bound parts into a separate **evaluation** layer. Don't let the messiness of one bleed into the cleanliness of the other.

Pushed further, you get **three nested layers**, ordered by how verifiable they are — evaluation on the outside, a verifiable core of data and pure math at the center:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph eval[Evaluation: judgment-bound, trust-dependent]
    subgraph est[Estimation: models & calculation]
      core[Data & pure math:<br/>verifiable]
    end
  end
```

1. **Verifiable** — raw data, mathematical facts, proofs.
2. **Estimation** — derived numbers from models and calculation.
3. **Evaluation** — the irreducibly judgment-bound calls.

The heuristic: *do as much work as possible in the deeper (more verifiable) layers, and keep the layers separate.* Every claim you can demote from "evaluation" to "estimation," and from "estimation" to "verifiable," gets cheaper and easier to keep consistent at scale.

Demotion does not remove judgment; it moves it into the model's structure, weights and inputs. A cost-effectiveness model turns "how good is this charity?" into arithmetic, but its moral weights and discount rate are still evaluations. The gain is that the judgment becomes explicit and separately contestable. The risk, familiar from composite indicators, is false precision: a number that looks like an estimate and hides the value choices that drive it ([Adjacent Fields §3](/reference/adjacent-fields/#3-program-evaluation--impact-measurement)).

## Two notes on naming

- There is already an academic field called **Evaluation** (program evaluation, rooted in the social sciences). It overlaps with this usage but is centered on bespoke studies and long reports rather than high-throughput systems. We borrow lessons but reframe the scope.
- "Estimation" and "evaluation" are deliberately plain words, chosen as honest categories rather than branding. They still collide with existing usage: program evaluation (above) and AI "evals" ([Chapter 1](/start-here/introduction/#not-ai-model-evals-though-they-overlap)). Better names may come later.

## Where this goes

The estimation/evaluation split is what makes the [component architecture](/concepts/components/) coherent: *prediction* and *calculation* mostly serve the estimation layer, *evaluation methods* serve the evaluation layer, and *ontology* organizes the questions both operate on. The system-level [techniques](/concepts/techniques/) — especially prediction–evaluation systems — are largely about cheaply bridging the two.


------------------------------------------------------------
## 3. Why It Matters — Use Cases
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/start-here/use-cases/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, revised October 2026. The first section uses deployed or tested systems; the second keeps the founding posts' speculative cases, which never shipped.*

The point of an evaluation system is end-to-end value: resources in, better decisions out. An accurate evaluation that nobody acts on is worth nothing, so the motivating question is which decisions improve when adequate evaluations get cheap.

## Cases with real systems behind them

**Grant portfolios.** Many funders read closely only the grants a program officer has time for; the rest are renewed on momentum. The [worked example](/concepts/worked-example/) prices four designs for a funder with 1,000 grants a year and shows what a 50-item audit can and cannot establish.

**Research triage.** DARPA's SCORE program priced the replicability of claims from about 3,000 papers and validated the forecasts against a small replicated subset; human forecasts carried real signal and AI imitators did not ([Lineage](/start-here/lineage/#outside-precedents-for-the-core-pattern)). A cheap replicability prior over a literature is useful to funders, reviewers and meta-analysts even when it is wrong on many individual claims.

**Peer review.** At AAAI-26 every main-track paper received a labelled AI review alongside the human ones, and surveyed authors and committee members preferred it on most criteria while about half of committee respondents said it missed points a human would have caught ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#what-the-judge-literature-measures)). Review is the clearest live case of an LLM taking a slot in a judgment-bound evaluation system, and of the gaming that follows: hidden "positive review only" prompts turned up in arXiv preprints in 2025 ([evidence](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#evidence-under-optimization-pressure)).

## Charity evaluation and prioritization

This is the case closest to the founding notes. GiveWell, Open Philanthropy, 80,000 Hours and others put serious effort into evaluating charities and causes, and it has been hard to scale; there are perennial calls for a "GiveWell for X".

The framing here is augmentation, not replacement:

> for every prioritization or evaluation researcher we have, can we eventually get x% more value out of them?

A system that let existing teams cover far more questions at lower per-item quality could change which questions get asked at all. How large that multiplier is has not been measured. Small instances exist: QURI's [shallow evaluations of longtermist organizations](/reference/related-work/) (2021) and Sam Nolan's uncertainty-quantified rebuild of GiveWell's GiveDirectly analysis. The strongest skeptical reply, that even perfect evaluations might not more than double useful work because the binding constraint is capable people, is in [Objections & FAQ](/reference/objections/#external-commentary).

## The founding posts' speculative cases

The 2021–22 notes motivated the field with mechanisms that each need cheap, trusted estimates at scale. None has been deployed at meaningful scale, so they show what the field would enable rather than demand for it.

- **Futarchy.** Hanson's proposal ([drafted from 2000, published 2013](https://mason.gmu.edu/~rhanson/futarchy2013.pdf)) to "vote on values, bet on beliefs" needs a welfare metric that resists corruption and policy forecasts cheap enough to commission routinely. Both are evaluation problems whatever the forecasting mechanism.
- **Certificates of impact.** [Christiano's 2014 proposal](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/yNn2o3kEhixZHkRga/certificates-of-impact), trialled with Katja Grace as the 2015 [Impact Purchase](https://impactpurchase.org/certificates-of-impact/), needs value estimates for many projects, and faces the candidness problem: publicly priced impact gives organizations reason to withhold their weaker work ([Epistemic Culture](/concepts/epistemic-culture/#the-candidness-problem)).
- **General cost–benefit calculators.** QALYs and welfare economics put numbers on acts in narrow domains. A general calculator for individuals and organizations would need cheap large-scale estimation, and probably a way to plug in different value functions; nobody has shown that is feasible.
- **Estimation tooling.** Guesstimate (2016) made uncertain estimation accessible and then hit diminishing returns; the later bet is on composable [estimation functions](/concepts/techniques/) and LLM-generated models such as Squiggle AI ([Related Work](/reference/related-work/)).

## The common thread

None of these needs near-perfect accuracy. Each needs outputs better than what decision-makers would otherwise have used, at a cost low enough that they get used, and robust enough that they survive the evaluated caring about them. See [Evaluation as a System](/concepts/the-systems-view/) for the design target and [Objections & FAQ](/reference/objections/) for the case against.


------------------------------------------------------------
## 4. Cruxes
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/start-here/key-questions/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, updated October 2026. Numbers are stable; other pages cite them.*

A crux is a question where a confident answer would redirect effort. Each entry says what evidence exists as of late 2026. The longer, per-chapter list is [Open Problems](/open-questions/).

## On the premise

1. **Is the bottleneck the system, not the estimate?** The founding bet is that we can make one good evaluation and fail at making ten thousand cheaply. In domains where experts barely agree with each other (grant review is one), single-evaluation quality may still be the binding constraint.
2. **Does scale unlock value, or just volume?** Ten thousand mediocre estimates may be worth less than ten excellent ones. As far as this wiki knows, no study yet shows a high-throughput system for judging grants, organizations or policies changing decisions that would not otherwise have changed.

## On estimation vs. evaluation

3. **How much can be demoted from evaluation to estimation?** Divide and conquer is only as good as the fraction of judgment-bound questions that can be turned into model-bound ones. No one has estimated that fraction for any real portfolio.
4. **Can LLMs do trustworthy evaluation, or only cheap evaluation?** Agreement with human panels is now measured for chat responses, essays, clinical rubrics and paper review, and at AAAI-26 every main-track paper received an AI review, which surveyed authors and committee members found useful ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#what-the-judge-literature-measures)). None of that measures normative, long-horizon judgment, and none of it measures trust in the accountability sense: whether people accept an unappealable model verdict.

## On the components

5. **Does scalable structured forecasting work?** Can we forecast over large structured ontologies ("for each country, each month, 20 metrics, 20 years") without quality collapsing, now that LLM forecasters make the volume cheap?
6. **Is ontology the silent bottleneck?** Is structuring the questions the hard part, more than answering them?
7. **What is the right interface for estimation functions?** If the unit of reuse is a cached function from parameters to an estimate, what tooling lets these compose at scale?

## On bridging cheap and expensive judgment

8. **Do prediction–evaluation systems calibrate cheap predictors?** Partly answered. In DARPA's SCORE program, human forecasters predicting replication outcomes reached an AUC of about 0.76 against 37 audited replications, while AI systems built to imitate the human judgments failed to discriminate ([Lineage](/start-here/lineage/#outside-precedents-for-the-core-pattern)). Open: whether the pattern survives deceptive participants and evaluated parties who optimize against the cheap layer, and whether it works when the expensive evaluator is a panel's judgment rather than a replication.
9. **How do you price an evaluation?** Trading accuracy against cost needs a value-of-information story for messy, normative, long-horizon questions. The sibling wiki's [Core Model](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/core-model/) offers one; it has not been applied to a real portfolio.

## On the environment

10. **Is culture the real adoption bottleneck?** Documented cases show the evaluated exiting (the 2022 US News law-school boycott) and an inspectorate losing its coarsest output (Ofsted's single-word grades, removed in 2024) ([Epistemic Culture](/concepts/epistemic-culture/)). Whether such pushback binds harder than technical limits, and whether it is more tractable, is unknown.
11. **Does payment buy the evaluator, or mark high stakes?** A coding of 161 catalogued systems found that neither payer type nor method predicted documented failure, but systems paid by the parties they rate had about 3.5 times the odds of one ([catalogue](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/#does-who-pays-predict-failure)). Most of those failures were gaming by the rated party rather than lenient rating, which fits either reading. If payment buys the evaluator, the main work is designing payer and governance; if it marks stakes, the main work is robustness to gaming.

## On the field itself

12. **Is "evaluation engineering" the right frame and name?** The lineage went from advanced evaluation systems through estimation systems to the present framing. The name also collides with AI-model "evals" ([Chapter 1](/start-here/introduction/#not-ai-model-evals-though-they-overlap)). Renaming would avoid confusion; keeping it claims the overlap with a large, funded community.
13. **Does shared infrastructure make errors systemic?** If many funders adopt the same few LLM judges, their mistakes may correlate across institutions, so that the same applicants are rejected everywhere ([Kleinberg & Raghavan 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.05853); [Bommasani et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.13972)). Scaled evaluation may need deliberate diversity of judges, which costs some of the savings.

---

Candidate answers, and cruxes this list is missing, are the contribution this wiki most wants.


================================================================================
# Part I — The Systems View
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## 5. Evaluation as a System
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/the-systems-view/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, revised October 2026.*

## A system is not a big pile of evaluations

An evaluation is an artifact: a number, a grade, a report. An **evaluation system** is the standing machinery that produces such artifacts repeatedly, of a roughly consistent type: a health department grading restaurants, an analyst team scoring acquisition targets, a charity evaluator publishing cost-effectiveness estimates. Each lives or dies on properties no single evaluation has: cost per item, consistency across items, how it absorbs change, and whether the people it rates can bend it.

Optimizing a system means accepting that some outputs are rougher than a bespoke study, in exchange for producing enough of them, cheaply enough, that they get used.

Program evaluation has studied such standing "evaluation systems" (performance monitoring, accreditation, institutionalized impact evaluation) and names a cost of them: they tend to produce routinized information that serves day-to-day adjustment but rarely prompts a fundamental reassessment of a programme ([Leeuw & Furubo 2008](https://doi.org/10.1177/1356389007087537)). A high-throughput design inherits that risk.

## The design space

Four properties decide whether a system is worth running:

- **Accuracy**: how close outputs come to what a much more expensive, trusted process would conclude, measured on a random audit ([Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/)). This is agreement with a reference, not validity: a system that matches a biased panel inherits the bias, and the audit cannot see it.
- **Unit cost**: a fixed cost $F$ (design, calibration, tooling, re-validation) plus a marginal cost $c$ per item. Quantity $N$ is the scale the system runs at, not a separate axis: total cost is $F + Nc$.
- **Robustness to gaming**: whether accuracy survives once the evaluated learn what the system rewards. A judge validated at zero optimization pressure is validated only for zero pressure ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#evidence-under-optimization-pressure)).
- **Legitimacy**: whether the audience trusts the outputs enough to act on them and the evaluated accept them enough not to exit, sue or capture the system. Trust is evaluation's [defining requirement](/start-here/estimation-vs-evaluation/#evaluation).

Earlier drafts used a three-way "accuracy × quantity × cost" trade-off. It double-counted (total cost is quantity times unit cost) and left out robustness and legitimacy.

As accounting, a system run over $N$ items is worth roughly $N\bar{v} - (F + Nc)$, where $\bar{v}$ is the average decision value an output adds. Because the most decision-relevant items tend to be evaluated first, $\bar{v}$ usually falls as $N$ grows; scale pays up to the item whose value drops to $c$, and only if the total covers $F$. Accuracy enters through $\bar{v}$, and so does latency: a verdict that arrives after the decision is worth little. Robustness and legitimacy act as multipliers on $\bar{v}$: a gamed output, or one nobody believes, has $\bar{v}$ near zero, and a system that loses legitimacy may lose $N$ as well when the evaluated refuse to take part ([Epistemic Culture](/concepts/epistemic-culture/)). The sibling RRP wiki's [Core Model](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/core-model/) develops the same unit economics and how to price information before it is produced.

The properties trade against each other in recognizable ways. An expert panel buys accuracy and legitimacy at a high marginal cost. A statistical index has a low marginal cost, is accurate only where the metric captures what matters, and is among the easiest designs to game. LLMs cut the marginal cost of the labor-intensive steps; whether robustness and legitimacy survive the substitution is open ([Cruxes](/start-here/key-questions/)).

## The questions that define a system

Designing or critiquing a system means answering, at minimum:

- **Team.** Who produces the judgments (analysts, experts, crowds, models), and at what cost per item?
- **Data.** Where do inputs come from, how fresh are they, and does the system depend on the evaluated to supply them?
- **Audience and purpose.** Who consumes the outputs, and what decisions do they support? This sets how much accuracy is needed.
- **Consistency and propagation.** How do thousands of outputs stay coherent, and how does a changed input reach everything downstream?
- **Audit.** What expensive, trusted process checks a random sample, and how often?
- **Payer and governance.** Who funds the system, who controls the metric's definition, and what recourse do the evaluated have?

Consistency and propagation make an evaluation system resemble a database with opinions; payer and governance make it resemble an institution.

## Technical and institutional design variables

The questions above mix two kinds of variable. Team, data pipeline, consistency, propagation and audit are **technical**: they are set by how the system is built. Payer, metric ownership, disclosure and appeal are **institutional**: they are set by the contracts and governance around it.

Certification economics predicts that the institutional variables matter: a certifier paid by the rated party prefers coarse, lenient signals, and issuer-pays invites ratings shopping ([Patterns §3](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#3-incentives-and-funding-shape-trustworthiness)). A coding of the catalogue's 161 systems gives partial support ([Does who pays predict failure?](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/#does-who-pays-predict-failure)). Neither the payer typology nor method predicted documented failure. One contrast held: where the rated party pays the evaluator anything, 27 of 67 systems had an established failure, against 10 of 62 where it pays nothing (odds ratio about 3.5, 90% CI 1.6–7.8). Most of those failures were gaming by the rated party, not lenient rating, so payment may mark high-stakes ratings rather than buy the evaluator. The evidence is weak: one unblinded coder, and only failures someone documented.

The institutional choices are:

- **Payer.** Rated party pays (credit ratings, fee-for-certification), audience pays (subscriptions), a third party pays (foundation, government, a funder evaluating its own grantees), or advertisers and affiliates pay. Each has a known conflict; the [catalogue](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/) groups systems this way. A funder evaluating its own portfolio has the mildest external conflict and the strongest internal one: the evaluators report to the people whose decisions they judge.
- **Metric ownership.** Whoever defines the metric can move it. Keeping the definition with a party that does not benefit from its level is the analogue of auditor independence.
- **Data independence.** A system that gathers its own inputs cannot be starved of them; one that relies on self-reported data can be boycotted or fed false numbers.
- **Disclosure.** Publishing the method makes the system auditable and also easier to game. A common compromise is to publish the rubric and keep the audit sample and the model's exact prompts private ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-design-pattern-llms-as-the-cheap-layer)).
- **Appeal and aggregation rules.** Recourse for the evaluated buys legitimacy at some cost to throughput. Aggregation rules can be designed for legitimacy directly: X's Community Notes shows a note only when raters who usually disagree both rate it helpful, and in a field test such notes reduced resharing ([Wojcik et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.15723)). The price is latency: once attached, notes cut a post's reposts by 46%, but by only 12% over its lifetime, because most sharing happens before a note qualifies ([Slaughter et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2503413122)).

These are engineering choices in the sense that matters: they can be specified in advance, varied, and measured. A system is specified by its payer and governance as much as by its pipeline.

## Consistency and propagation

At small scale, inconsistency is invisible. At ten thousand items it becomes a dominant failure: estimate A implies one thing, estimate B its opposite, and nobody reads both. A serious system needs shared inputs, derived-value chains or automated checks that make "these two outputs contradict each other" a detectable event; the sibling wiki's [consistency evals](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/proposals/consistency-evals/) catalogue such checks.

Propagation is the dynamic version. A key input changes, and in a pile of static reports every downstream conclusion is silently stale. A system that knows what depends on what can re-derive or flag the affected outputs. This is the main argument for [estimation functions](/concepts/techniques/) and structured ontologies over free-text reports.

## Grading systems: a capability ladder

If the system is the unit of design, systems should be gradable, as autonomous driving has "Level 4". The [Capability Ladder](/concepts/capability-ladder/) proposes five rungs, each defined by a test: standardized, measured, monitored, gaming-tested, accountable. The last is the institutional variables above. The [Launch Checklist](/concepts/launch-checklist/) turns the rungs into steps. The founding notes called systems high on such a ladder "advanced": cost-effective, general, and valuable to the agents that consume their outputs.


------------------------------------------------------------
## 6. The Four Components
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/components/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, adapted from the 2021–22 estimation-theory notes.*

An evaluation system decomposes into four reusable parts. Each has its own literature, tooling and failure modes, which is the reason to separate them. [Techniques](/concepts/techniques/) covers how they are wired together; [epistemic culture](/concepts/epistemic-culture/) is a precondition for running any of them, not a part.

## Prediction

Probabilistic forecasts that can be scored against outcomes and aggregated, in the sense of Tetlock & Gardner's *Superforecasting* (2015). Scoring gives the system a feedback signal; aggregation lets it combine many cheap judgments. Human prediction without calculation is limited to what people can intuit, which suffices for hundreds of hand-written questions and not for thousands. LLM forecasters lift the volume limit at a shrinking cost in accuracy ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#what-llms-cheapen-component-by-component)).

## Calculation

The multi-step machinery that turns inputs into derived numbers: Fermi chains, models, spreadsheets, algorithms. This is the engine of the [estimation](/start-here/estimation-vs-evaluation/) layer. Calculation without prediction produces elaborate numbers with no evidence of calibration. Prediction supplies trust, calculation supplies reach; the boundary between them is fuzzy, but separating them helps both research and software design.

## Ontology

The structured list of things the system estimates, and the data plumbing beneath it: taxonomies, definitions, knowledge graphs. Large structured item sets are what let a system predict or calculate over thousands of questions. The founding notes flagged this as the neglected bottleneck, since forecasting platforms mostly rely on small sets of hand-written questions. That has started to change: ForecastBench generates and refreshes its 1,000 forecasting questions automatically ([Karger et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19839)). Whether automated question generation extends from resolvable forecasts to evaluation targets is open.

## Evaluation

Judgment on questions that are normative, long-horizon or otherwise lack clean ground truth: the residue the estimation layer cannot reduce. Evaluation counts only if its audience believes it, so it depends on legitimacy more than the other components do. It is usually the *target* of prediction: the expensive, trusted judgment that cheaper predictors are scored against. The concrete methods are compared on [Evaluation Methods](/concepts/evaluation-methods/).

## Dependencies

Ontology defines the questions. Calculation and prediction populate the estimation layer over them. Evaluation handles what cannot be estimated and supplies the ground truth that prediction is scored against. The integration is not a thin layer: keeping thousands of outputs consistent across components, and propagating updates between them, is where large systems fail ([Evaluation as a System](/concepts/the-systems-view/#consistency-and-propagation)).


================================================================================
# Part II — Methods & Techniques
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## 7. Evaluation Methods
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/evaluation-methods/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, October 2026. Costs are given as structure (fixed vs. marginal) unless a source prices them. Measured reliabilities come from the cited studies and do not transfer automatically to a new domain.*

The [evaluation component](/concepts/components/#evaluation) needs a method. Each method below is a point in the [design space](/concepts/the-systems-view/#the-design-space) of accuracy, unit cost, robustness and legitimacy. [Evaluation Systems in the Wild](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/) shows each deployed; the [capability ladder](/concepts/capability-ladder/) grades systems built from them.

| Method | What it measures | Known failure modes | Cost structure | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Expert panel / peer review** | expert judgment of quality or merit | low inter-rater agreement (mean κ ≈ 0.17 across 48 studies); outcome depends on which reviewers are drawn | high marginal: reviewer time, over 100M hours globally in 2020, valued at over \$1.5B for US-based reviewers alone | [Bornmann et al. 2010](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0014331); [Pier et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1714379115); [Aczel et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1186/s41073-021-00118-2) |
| **Structured expert elicitation** (Cooke's classical model; Delphi, IDEA) | calibrated quantities and uncertainty from experts | under a third of experts were statistically accurate across 33 classical-model studies; performance weighting beat equal weighting on combined score in 31 of 33 (in-sample) | high fixed (seed questions, facilitation) per study | [Colson & Cooke 2018](https://doi.org/10.1093/reep/rex022); see the sibling [elicitation guide](https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/design-patterns/tools/expert-elicitation/) |
| **Structured appraisal tools** (GRADE, Cochrane RoB 2) | conformance of a study or evidence body to a checklist | checklist judgments still diverge: four expert raters reached κ 0.16 on RoB 2's overall judgment | about 28 min per trial outcome per rater | [Minozzi et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2020.06.015) |
| **Survey** | opinion of a defined population, e.g. a forecast's actual readers | nonresponse bias, which response rate predicts poorly; question wording | moderate marginal per respondent | [Groves & Peytcheva 2008](https://doi.org/10.1093/poq/nfn011) |
| **Crowd ratings / reviews** | self-selected users' satisfaction | J-shaped self-selection; herding on early votes; fake reviews, reduced but not removed by verified-purchase rules | high fixed (platform, moderation), near-zero marginal | [Patterns §2](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#2-the-ratings-you-collect-are-a-biased-sample), [§4](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#4-reputation-systems-converge-on-the-same-arms-race) |
| **Statistical indicator** | a measurable proxy | Goodhart and surrogation once the indicator carries stakes; measures what is convenient | low marginal once data exist | [Patterns §1](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#1-the-measure-reshapes-the-measured) |
| **Composite index** | a broad construct from weighted indicators | arbitrary weights; manipulation of inputs: the World Bank's *Doing Business* was discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities | moderate fixed, low marginal | [World Bank 2021](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/statement/2021/09/16/world-bank-group-to-discontinue-doing-business-report) |
| **Inspection / independent testing** | compliance or performance against a standard | snapshot validity; works when the metric is hard to game and demand responds (LA hygiene grade cards) | high marginal per inspection | [Jin & Leslie 2003](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/118/2/409/1899578) |
| **Impact evaluation** (RCTs, quasi-experiments) | an intervention's causal effect on chosen outcomes | effects vary widely across contexts, so results transfer poorly; across 600+ development studies, government-run programs showed smaller effects than academic- or NGO-run ones | high fixed per study | [Vivalt 2020](https://doi.org/10.1093/jeea/jvaa019) |
| **Forecasting resolved by an evaluator** (markets, polls) | predicted outcome of an expensive evaluation | thin incentives when few items resolve; accuracy must be read against the base rate (markets called 73% of 104 replication outcomes) | low marginal per item, plus a resolution budget | [Liu et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04543); [Techniques](/concepts/techniques/#predictionevaluation-systems) |
| **Pairwise comparison** (Bradley–Terry, arenas) | relative preference | order effects in online Elo; cyclic preferences; selective disclosure of privately tested variants | low marginal per vote | [Singh et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879); [Patterns §5](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#5-the-scale-and-the-aggregation-rule-are-not-neutral) |
| **LLM judge** | predicted human judgment | agreement with humans varies by task and item difficulty; position, verbosity and self-preference bias; prompt sensitivity; correlated errors across models; null responses and adversarial phrases inflate scores | very low marginal; fixed cost of validation and re-validation dominates | [LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/); [Zheng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07137) |

## Reading the table

Two regularities stand out. First, the methods with the highest standing (peer review, appraisal tools) have some of the lowest measured agreement; their legitimacy comes from who does them, not from measured accuracy. These are single-rater figures, though. Averaging helps: by the Spearman–Brown formula, peer review's mean single-rater ICC of .34 implies about .61 for the mean of three interchangeable reviewers. And reviewers are often chosen for different expertise, so part of the disagreement may be by design. Second, the cheap methods (indicators, indices, crowd ratings, LLM judges) fail mainly under optimization pressure, so their unattacked accuracy overstates their deployed accuracy. A system usually pairs one of each: a cheap method on every item, audited by an expensive one on a sample (the [prediction–evaluation pattern](/concepts/techniques/#predictionevaluation-systems)). High-stakes essay scoring runs a more cautious pairing, with a human on every item and the machine as a check ([capability ladder](/concepts/capability-ladder/#eight-systems-graded)).

Not every method answers the whole question. Surveys, indicators, appraisal checklists and impact evaluations are often **partial evaluations**: inputs to a fuller judgment rather than substitutes for it. Designing a system means deciding which items get full evaluation and which ride on partial measures plus prediction.

## Open territory

- **Elicitation.** How to phrase questions so evaluators answer the intended one, and how to elicit value judgments. QURI's relative value functions and the sibling RRP wiki's [Constructing Utility Functions](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/constructing-utility-functions/) are concrete attempts.
- **Pricing.** Few methods have published cost per item; most rows above give structure, not numbers. A system cannot trade accuracy against cost without them.
- **Deployed LLM evaluators.** RRP's [LLM Epistemics in Production](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/case-studies/llm-epistemics-in-production/) documents RoastMyPost and Squiggle AI, including their false-positive problems.


------------------------------------------------------------
## 8. Techniques
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/techniques/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, adapted from the 2021–22 estimation-theory notes. Each technique carries a status: **tested** (measured in a controlled or deployed setting), **deployed elsewhere** (in use, but not as proposed here), or **untested**.*

The [components](/concepts/components/) are the parts; these are ways to wire them into a system. Most answer one question: how can a small amount of expensive, trusted judgment discipline a large amount of cheap judgment?

## Prediction–evaluation systems

*Status: tested.*

Ask predictors to forecast a large set of items, say 10,000, and announce that a random subset, say 50, will be resolved by an expensive, trusted [evaluation](/concepts/evaluation-methods/). Reward accuracy on that subset. Because no predictor knows which items will be graded, each must treat every item as if it might be. A small evaluation budget then calibrates forecasts across the whole set. What gets calibrated is agreement with the evaluator, errors included: predictors are paid to model the evaluator, not the truth.

The incentive thins as the set grows: with 50 of 10,000 resolved, each item has a 1-in-200 chance of counting. A proper scoring rule stays proper under random resolution, but the reward for effort on any one item falls by that factor.

The pattern can chain. Calibrated human predictions become training labels for cheaper ML predictors, which are audited against a fresh subset, and so on. Whether each step loses little accuracy has not been measured, and errors compound across steps.

The evidence runs in both directions. The idea was written up as [*Prediction-Augmented Evaluation Systems*](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/kMmNdHpQPcnJgnAQF/prediction-augmented-evaluation-systems) (2018) and tested in [*Amplifying generalist research via forecasting*](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/ZTXKHayPexA6uSZqE/part-2-amplifying-generalist-research-via-forecasting) (2019). There, 19 forecasters predicting a trusted evaluator recovered 87% of the value of her direct evaluation at 120% of her cost; cheaper crowdworkers, at 52% of the cost, recovered negative value. The authors framed it as an existence proof, not a cost-effectiveness result.

The largest tests use replication as the expensive evaluator. Across four forecasting studies run alongside replication projects, prediction markets called 73% of 104 replication outcomes correctly, and surveys of the same participants did somewhat worse; accuracy has to be read against each project's replication base rate ([Liu et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04543), summarizing [Dreber et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1516179112) and three later studies). DARPA's SCORE program then had forecasters price about 3,000 social- and behavioural-science publications, of which about 250 would be replicated, using decision markets and surrogate scoring rules to keep incentives intact when most forecasts would never resolve (same source). When no item will ever resolve, peer-prediction mechanisms score each report against the others; the Bayesian truth serum rewards answers that are more common than respondents collectively predicted, which makes truth-telling optimal even for a minority view ([Prelec 2004](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1102081)). The guarantee needs a large population of Bayesian respondents with a common prior, and truth-telling is an equilibrium, not the only one. The statistics for turning many cheap predictions plus a random audited subset into valid estimates is [prediction-powered inference](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#prediction-powered-inference).

Open: whether the incentive survives gaming by the *evaluated* party rather than the predictors ([LLMs as Evaluators, step 3](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-design-pattern-llms-as-the-cheap-layer)), and what happens when participants are deceptive (see [Cruxes](/start-here/key-questions/) and the sibling RRP wiki's [oversight protocols](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/oversight-protocols/) and [untrustworthy sources](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/untrustworthy-sources/)).

## Forecasting over structured ontologies

*Status: deployed elsewhere, at benchmark scale.*

Many questions worth forecasting are structured: "for each country, each month for 20 years, what will each of 20 metrics be?" Judgmental platforms, built around hand-written questions, handle this poorly. Automated generation from data sources now produces question sets in the thousands ([ForecastBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19839)), but continuous, high-dimensional forecasting at that scale remains a tooling problem that leans on the [ontology](/concepts/components/#ontology) component.

## Estimation functions

*Status: deployed elsewhere; value at scale untested.*

A function that returns estimates over large parameter sets, usually with caching: the unit of reuse for the [estimation](/start-here/estimation-vs-evaluation/) layer. It needs tooling for uncertainty, composition and dependency tracking. [Squiggle](https://www.squiggle-language.com/) is one attempt, and [Squiggle AI](/reference/related-work/) is a deployed LLM front-end that writes such models, with documented overconfidence. The [*Scorable Functions*](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/otFDNWGN3zhNXXGrH/scorable-functions-a-format-for-algorithmic-forecasting) (2024) proposal should be read with the author's later [comment](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/ZWQ5jbLxpd4JtQgu4/scorable-functions-a-format-for-algorithmic-forecasting) that he had "become much less enamored by this broad idea", expecting people to ask LLMs for estimates on demand instead.

Their systems value is [propagation](/concepts/the-systems-view/#consistency-and-propagation): if estimates are composable functions of shared inputs, an updated input flows through to everything downstream instead of leaving stale reports.

## Automated trust networks

*Status: untested in this form; simpler trust networks are deployed.*

Central evaluators are single points of capture: issuer-paid credit ratings before 2008, and the World Bank's *Doing Business* index, discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities ([Patterns §3](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#3-incentives-and-funding-decide-trustworthiness--more-than-method-does)). The proposed alternative is many agencies that evaluate the large ones and each other. A stronger version lets an agency publish declared corrections to another's outputs: X accepts Y's economic forecasts but shades Y's steel-industry forecasts for overconfidence. "Whom do you trust" becomes inspectable structure rather than a binary. The simpler form, where trust propagates through a graph of ratings, has long been deployed: EigenTrust computes global trust in peer-to-peer networks from local ratings and resists simulated collusion among malicious peers ([Kamvar, Schlosser & Garcia-Molina 2003](https://doi.org/10.1145/775152.775242)). Declared corrections are what has not been tried. The sibling RRP wiki develops the identity layer this needs in [identity and track records](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/environment/identity-and-track-records/).

## Robust aggregation

*Status: deployed elsewhere.*

How raw judgments become a score is never neutral ([Patterns §5](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#5-the-scale-and-the-aggregation-rule-are-not-neutral)). Defaults with evidence behind them:

- Regularize sparse items: a Wilson lower bound for binary votes, Bayesian shrinkage for scores.
- Prefer pairwise comparison when raters are noisy; QURI's [relative value functions](/reference/related-work/#evaluation-methods--utility-elicitation) add uncertainty to the idea.
- For probability forecasts, average log-odds rather than probabilities, and consider extremizing the result: averaging probabilities pulls toward 0.5, and each forecaster's confidence ignores evidence others hold ([Baron et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1287/deca.2014.0293)).
- Pool with a median or trimmed mean, which one bad input cannot drag far; RRP develops this as [breakdown-point ratings](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/hardening-invariance/#worked-bound).
- Tie each rating to a verified purchase, stay or identity, the recurring fix for fake and brigaded ratings ([Patterns §4](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#4-reputation-systems-converge-on-the-same-arms-race)).

Candidness, which the 2021–22 notes listed as a technique, is a precondition for deployment and has [its own chapter](/concepts/epistemic-culture/). For the operational sequence of standing up a system, see the [Launch Checklist](/concepts/launch-checklist/).


------------------------------------------------------------
## 9. LLMs as Evaluators
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/llm-evaluators/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: early draft, September 2026; evidence sections revised October 2026. How to measure a judge (chance-corrected agreement, baselines, error bars, prediction-powered inference, gaming tests) is in [Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/). This chapter develops the claim the whole wiki rests on: that LLMs are the cheap, general executor the 2021–22 program lacked (see [Lineage](/start-here/lineage/)). Background citations are in the [LLM-evaluation section](/reference/adjacent-fields/#4-llm-based-evaluation--ai-evals) of Adjacent Fields.*

## The claim, and what would falsify it

The founding program stalled on labor. Its architecture needed someone to draft evaluations, structure ontologies, and run calculations for thousands of items, and paying analysts for that made the whole system too expensive to run at scale. The "why now" of this wiki is that language models do much of that labor at a small fraction of the cost.

Stated as a testable claim: **for a given class of evaluation questions, an LLM-based evaluator agrees with a trusted panel about as often as a second, independent panel would, at a cost per item at least ten times lower, and keeps that agreement on audited items after months of deployment, when the evaluated parties have had time to optimize against it.** The claim is falsified for a question class if post-deployment LLM–panel agreement on randomly audited items falls clearly below panel–panel agreement.

The evidence is uneven across the three parts. Accuracy and cost are well supported for *checkable* or chat-style tasks: code that runs, forecasts that resolve, preferences between chat responses. For judgment without ground truth, the closest measurements come from automated essay scoring and LLM review of research papers; normative, long-horizon judgment is largely unmeasured. On the third part the direct evidence is negative: undefended LLM judges have been gamed in the lab and in the wild (below). That part decides whether LLM evaluation is engineering or a demo.

## What LLMs cheapen, component by component

Mapped onto [the four components](/concepts/components/):

| Component | What an LLM does | State of the evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Ontology** | drafts structured question sets, definitions, resolution criteria | cheap to generate; quality control is the bottleneck. LLM-authored questions skew toward ambiguous entities and timeframes |
| **Calculation** | writes and debugs estimation code | deployed: [Squiggle AI](/reference/related-work/#estimation--calculation-tooling) generates probabilistic models at \$0.10–0.35 per workflow, with documented systematic overconfidence |
| **Prediction** | forecasts directly, or predicts an expensive evaluator | on ForecastBench the best LLM systems trailed superforecasters by 0.017 difficulty-adjusted Brier points in January 2026, about a year of LLM progress at the recent rate ([Karger et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19839); [FRI 2026](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/llms-are-closing-the-gap-on-human)) |
| **Evaluation** | judges quality, scores against rubrics, critiques documents | the most-studied use: the LLM-as-judge literature below; deployed as [RoastMyPost](/reference/related-work/#evaluation-methods--utility-elicitation), whose authors report a "significant" false-positive rate |

The pattern across the column: the cost per call is similar everywhere, but LLM output is cheapest to *validate* where it can be checked. Code runs or fails; forecasts resolve; a rubric score does not check itself. So the accuracy-vs-cost question has to be asked separately for each component, and it is hardest for evaluation.

## What the judge literature measures

The research on LLMs as judges has moved from "can they judge?" to cataloguing how they fail:

- **Agreement.** On open-ended chat responses, a strong LLM judge agreed with human preferences about as often as humans agreed with each other: over 80% in the landmark study ([Zheng et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)). That is the accuracy half of the claim, for one task class.
- **Agreement depends on the task and on the item's difficulty.** Across 20 annotated NLP datasets, the same judges were reliable for some properties and poor for others ([Bavaresco et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18403)). Where humans agree closely with each other, only the largest judges aligned reasonably with them, still well short of human–human agreement, and judges tended to be lenient ([Thakur et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12624)). On expert-graded finance questions, judges without a reference answer agreed with experts mainly on questions the judges could answer themselves; an expert-written reference answer largely closed the gap ([Krumdick et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05061)). A judge validated on easy items is not validated on hard ones.
- **Biases that are truth-independent.** The same study names *position* bias (favoring whichever answer appears first), *verbosity* bias (favoring longer answers), and *self-enhancement* (favoring answers the judge generated itself; later work finds judges also favor models similar to themselves, [Goel et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313)). Each has a known partial fix: judge both orderings and average ([Wang et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17926)); regress out length ([Dubois et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04475)); use a judge from a different family.
- **Sensitivity to phrasing.** Meaning-preserving formatting changes alone can swing few-shot task accuracy by up to 76 points ([Sclar et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11324)). That result is for classification tasks, not judging, but judges run on the same prompt machinery. QURI's [opinion fuzzing](https://quantifieduncertainty.org/posts/opinion-fuzzing-a-proposal-for-reducing-exploring-variance-in-llm-judgments-via-sampling/) proposal treats this as something to measure: sample across prompts, models, and personas, and report the spread as the judgment's uncertainty.
- **Teams match the model and hallucinate less.** On catching bugs in real assistant code, trained critic models' critiques were preferred over human critiques 63% of the time, and human–model teams caught about as many bugs as the model alone while hallucinating fewer ([McAleese et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00215)). The cheapest reliable deployment may be making each expensive evaluator faster, not removing them. That is the use-case page's [augmentation framing](/start-here/use-cases/#charity-evaluation-and-prioritization), measured.
- **Judgment closer to evaluation.** Automated essay scoring has used machine–human against human–human agreement as its acceptance test for over a decade. A commonly applied criterion, attributed to [Williamson, Xi & Breyer (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3992.2011.00223.x), requires machine–human quadratic-weighted kappa to fall no more than 0.10 below human–human. On research papers, the points GPT-4 raised overlapped with human reviewers' points about as much as two human reviewers' overlapped with each other: 30.85% vs. 28.58% for Nature-family journals, 39.23% vs. 35.25% for ICLR ([Liang et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01783)). HealthBench scored its rubric grader against physicians as physicians are scored against each other, and it beat the average physician in five of seven themes ([Arora et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775); [details](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#the-human-panel-baseline)).
- **Deployed in review.** At AAAI-26 every one of 22,977 main-track papers received one labelled AI review, without scores or a recommendation, alongside the human reviews ([Biswas et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13940)). In a survey with 5,834 responses, authors and committee members preferred the AI reviews on six of nine criteria, including identifying technical errors, but also rated them somewhat more likely to contain technical errors themselves. About half of committee respondents (49.4%) said the AI review overlooked points a human would likely have caught. This measures perceived usefulness, not agreement with a panel's verdict.

None of these measures the normative, long-horizon judgments on the [evaluation side](/start-here/estimation-vs-evaluation/) of the field's core distinction, such as "how much did this organization reduce risk?", and none was measured while the evaluated parties optimized against the judge.

## Evidence under optimization pressure

The direct evidence is that undefended judges fail:

- **Null models win benchmarks.** A constant response, unrelated to the instruction, reached an 86.5% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0, 83.0 on Arena-Hard-Auto and 9.55 on MT-Bench ([Zheng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07137)).
- **Short strings inflate scores.** Universal adversarial phrases appended to a text push LLM judges toward maximum scores, transfer from a surrogate model to unseen judges, and work better against absolute scoring than against pairwise comparison ([Raina, Liusie & Gales 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14016)). In reference-based grading, bare symbols or openers such as "Thought process:" elicited false-positive rewards from many judges, including frontier models ([Zhao et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08794)). Nobody designed these: they surfaced when a policy trained by reinforcement learning against a Qwen2.5-72B judge collapsed to short reasoning openers that the judge kept rewarding.
- **In the wild.** In July 2025 Nikkei Asia [found hidden instructions](https://asia.nikkei.com/business/technology/artificial-intelligence/positive-review-only-researchers-hide-ai-prompts-in-papers), in white or tiny text, in 17 arXiv preprints from 14 institutions, telling AI reviewers to give positive reviews only. This is the evaluated party optimizing against the judge in a judgment-bound domain. It followed the spread of LLMs into reviewing: an estimated 6.5–16.9% of review text at four 2023–24 AI conferences was substantially LLM-modified ([Liang et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07183)).
- **Human judges degrade the same way.** RLHF made models better at convincing time-limited human evaluators without making them more correct, raising the evaluators' false-positive rate by 24.1% on a question-answering task and 18.3% on a programming task ([Wen et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12822)).
- **The process gets gamed, not only the judge.** On Chatbot Arena, a few providers privately tested many variants and could retract the scores they did not want; Meta tested 27 before the Llama 4 release. Best-of-k selection inflates scores even against an honest judge ([Singh et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879)).

Apart from training runs, these are proofs of concept against public or known judges. How fast a judge deployed on people degrades, and what defenses buy, is unmeasured.

## The two system-level failures

Per-item biases can be engineered around. Two failures show up only at the level of the whole system, which makes them this wiki's concern.

**1. Correlated error.** The standard move with a noisy judge is to average several. That works only if their errors are independent, and LLMs' are not: when two models are both wrong they tend to agree on the same wrong answer, far above chance ([Kim et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962)), and error similarity rises with capability ([Goel et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313)). So a panel of five models can deliver the *confidence* of five judges with the accuracy of fewer; how many fewer depends on correlation that has to be measured per task. Human expert panels are correlated too, but through different channels (shared training, groupthink). That makes mixing human and model judges a plausible way to buy independence that adding models cannot, though it is untested (see Open questions). The sibling RRP wiki calls correlated error [the field's largest undefended threat](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/hardening-techniques/#what-each-family-defends--and-the-gaps), and the Delegation Risk wiki [recomputes Kim et al.'s data](https://delegation-risk.quantifieduncertainty.org/entanglements/detection/correlation-calculator/#what-the-evidence-supports) on the scale needed to price stacked checks.

**2. Goodhart under optimization.** An LLM judge validated on a fixed test set is validated at zero optimization pressure. Deploy it as a gate that anything valuable depends on, and whoever is being evaluated starts optimizing against it. The evidence above shows that this happens; the reward-modeling literature shows the shape of what follows: as optimization against a proxy reward model increases, the proxy score keeps rising while the true objective (there, a larger "gold" reward model) first rises and then falls, both under reinforcement learning and under best-of-$n$ selection ([Gao, Schulman & Hilton 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760)). Best-of-$n$ is the closer analogue to an applicant drafting several versions of a report and submitting the one a public judge scores highest. The numbers don't transfer to report-writing; the pattern, proxy up and target eventually down, is [Goodhart's law](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#1-the-measure-reshapes-the-measured), and the same selection can be run as a [test](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#gaming-tests) before launch. The design consequence: **a judge's validity is indexed to the optimization pressure it was validated under.** Re-validate when the stakes attached to its scores rise, when the evaluated population changes, and whenever the underlying model is updated.

## The design pattern: LLMs as the cheap layer

Put together, these findings suggest one architecture, which is the [prediction–evaluation system](/concepts/techniques/#predictionevaluation-systems) with the cheap predictor now a model:

1. **Keep an expensive, trusted evaluator.** Humans, or a slow, heavily checked process. It is the reference the rest of the system is scored against.
2. **Have the LLM predict that evaluator** on every item, not judge in the abstract. "What would the panel say?" can be scored; "what is true?" often cannot. This makes the *question* scorable, not the answer true: the LLM inherits the panel's errors, and the panel is itself a target for the same optimization.
3. **Audit a hidden random subset** with the expensive evaluator. Random audits *measure* how much gaming is happening; by themselves they don't deter it. In [Techniques](/concepts/techniques/#predictionevaluation-systems), random resolution disciplines *predictors* because they are paid on the audited items. Here the gamer is the evaluated party, and if the model is public or queryable it can search for a winning report offline for almost nothing. Deterrence needs a penalty when an audit exposes gaming (disqualification, a forfeited deposit), which is the [inspection-game bound](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/hardening-deterrence/#worked-bounds) in the sibling wiki. Keeping the model and prompt private raises the cost of the offline search. The statistics for this step exist: prediction-powered inference combines the model's labels on every item with the audited subset to give confidence intervals that are valid whatever the model's quality, and narrower the better the model is ([Angelopoulos et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.09633)). The saving is bounded: a judge no more accurate than what it evaluates can at most halve the audits needed ([Dorner, Nastl & Hardt 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13341)).
4. **Report agreement against a second panel**, not against perfection or a single rater, and chance-corrected: two raters who both approve 80% of items agree 68% of the time by chance. A model predicting a panel's consensus can beat an individual rater just by averaging, so the fair bar is a held-out panelist against the rest ([Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#the-human-panel-baseline)). Two further caveats: where panels rarely agree, parity is easy and means little; and parity says nothing about *where* the errors fall. Weight agreement by decision impact (errors near the funding line matter most), and measure it on audited items after deployment, not only on a fixed pre-deployment set.
5. **Escalate disagreement.** Items where fuzzed prompts disagree, or where the model's confidence is low, go to the expensive layer first. Trust or Escalate formalizes this as a cascade: cheaper judges escalate to stronger ones when unsure, with a provable guarantee of a user-specified level of human agreement on the items the cascade does judge ([Jung, Brahman & Choi 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.18370)). The guarantee is statistical, tuned on a labelled calibration set, and holds for items that resemble that set. This catches *honest* uncertainty, not attacks: an input optimized against the model tends to produce a confident, consistent verdict, and a known escalation rule becomes one more target. Random audits (step 3) remain the only check on gaming.
6. **Re-validate on drift.** New model version, new stakes, or new population means a fresh audit sample before trusting old agreement numbers.

The [worked example](/concepts/worked-example/) puts numbers on this pattern for a grantmaking use case.

## What LLMs do not fix

Evaluation's defining requirement is that the audience [trusts the result](/start-here/estimation-vs-evaluation/#evaluation). Cheap judgments nobody believes move no decisions. A model can match a panel's accuracy and still carry none of its standing, because trust in an evaluator comes partly from accountability: a named panel can be questioned, blamed, and replaced. This is [crux 4](/start-here/key-questions/#on-estimation-vs-evaluation), and nothing in the literature above resolves it. Nor do LLMs change the [cultural constraint](/concepts/epistemic-culture/): a cheaper evaluator of people and organizations meets the same pushback, faster.

## Open questions

- Beyond essay scoring, paper review and clinical rubrics, for which *judgment-bound* questions has chance-corrected LLM–panel agreement been measured against panel–panel agreement?
- How fast does an LLM judge's accuracy decay as the evaluated parties start optimizing against it, and how large a penalty on audit failure is needed to slow the decay?
- How much independence does a mixed human–model panel buy over a model-only panel, per dollar?
- What audit fraction keeps a deployed LLM evaluator honest, as a function of the stakes attached to its scores? The sibling wiki's [inspection-game bound](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/hardening-deterrence/#worked-bounds) is one starting model.


------------------------------------------------------------
## 10. Measuring an Evaluator
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, October 2026. This chapter collects the measurement methods the rest of the wiki leans on. [LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/) argues for auditing a cheap judge against an expensive one; the [worked example](/concepts/worked-example/) applies the arithmetic to one case. Every number below that is not cited is computed in the text or in the snippet, and the simulated population in the snippet is illustrative.*

An evaluator is a measuring instrument, and the questions are the ones metrology asks of any instrument: does it give the same answer twice (reliability), does it measure the intended thing (validity), are its stated confidences honest (calibration), and how much does a measurement of all this cost in labelled items (sample size)? For an evaluator facing people who benefit from its verdicts there is a fifth: does it still work when they try to fool it?

## Reliability is not validity

*Reliability* is agreement of the evaluator with itself, or with interchangeable copies of itself: two runs of the same judge, two prompt phrasings, two reviewers drawn from the same pool. *Validity* is agreement with the thing the evaluation is meant to track. Reliability caps validity. In classical test theory the correlation of a score with *any* criterion is at most the square root of the score's reliability, so a judge whose repeated runs correlate at 0.5 cannot correlate above 0.71 with the truth, however good it is on average. Re-running an LLM judge under fuzzed prompts is therefore a cheap first measurement: it gives an upper bound on validity before a single expert label is bought. The bound is only as good as the perturbations. A judge run greedily on one prompt is close to perfectly reliable by construction; reliability has to be measured across the variations (phrasing, model version, item order) that deployment will actually introduce.

The converse fails. A judge can be perfectly reliable and wrong every time in the same way, and agreement between two models is mostly reliability: models share errors ([correlated error](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-two-system-level-failures)). Agreement with a human panel is a validity measure only to the extent the panel is the target. Usually it is a stand-in for something the funder actually cares about, such as whether the grant achieved anything. The panel can itself be unreliable or systematically wrong, as can benchmarks: a review of 445 LLM benchmarks found recurring validity weaknesses in what they measured, the tasks and the scoring ([Bean et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04703)), and [Salaudeen et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10573) match each kind of evaluation claim to the validity evidence it needs. The practical rule: write down what the panel stands in for, then decide which disagreements between panel and target the system can tolerate.

## Agreement, corrected for chance

Raw agreement $p_o$ is the share of items on which two raters give the same label. It is inflated by base rates: two raters who each independently say "yes" to 80% of items agree $0.8^2 + 0.2^2 = 68\%$ of the time without looking. Cohen's kappa subtracts the agreement expected from the raters' own marginal rates, $p_e$, and rescales:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

so that chance scores 0 and perfect agreement 1 ([Cohen 1960](https://doi.org/10.1177/001316446002000104)). The relatives:

- **Fleiss' κ** extends the idea to many raters: each item gets the same number of ratings, possibly from different raters ([Fleiss 1971](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0031619)).
- **Weighted κ** gives partial credit for near-misses on an ordinal scale. The quadratic-weighted version is the standard in automated essay scoring, whose acceptance test ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#what-the-judge-literature-measures)) compares machine–human against human–human weighted κ.
- **Krippendorff's α** works for any number of raters, any level of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio), and missing ratings ([Hayes & Krippendorff 2007](https://doi.org/10.1080/19312450709336664)). That makes it the default when the design is messy, as audit designs usually are.
- **ICC** (the intraclass correlation) plays the same role for continuous scores. Use the absolute-agreement form; the consistency form ignores a judge that scores every item a point high ([McGraw & Wong 1996](https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.1.1.30)).

Kappa has two well-known paradoxes ([Feinstein & Cicchetti 1990](https://doi.org/10.1016/0895-4356(90)90158-L)). Both follow from $p_e$ depending on the marginals:

| 2×2 table (yes-yes, yes-no, no-yes, no-no) | $p_o$ | $p_e$ | κ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40, 9, 6, 45 (balanced) | 0.85 | 0.50 | 0.70 |
| 80, 10, 5, 5 (raters' "yes" rates 90% and 85%) | 0.85 | 0.78 | 0.32 |
