| 45, 15, 25, 15 (raters' "yes" rates 60% and 70%) | 0.60 | 0.54 | 0.13 |
| 25, 35, 5, 35 (raters' "yes" rates 60% and 30%) | 0.60 | 0.46 | 0.26 |

- **Prevalence.** The first two rows have identical raw agreement. Kappa falls by more than half when both raters say "yes" to most items, because chance agreement is already high.
- **Bias.** In the last two rows, raters who disagree *more* about the base rate get the *higher* kappa, because their marginals predict less chance agreement.

Neither paradox is an error in kappa. Each is a reason not to report kappa alone. [Byrt, Bishop & Carlin (1993)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0895-4356(93)90018-V) recommend reporting prevalence and bias indices next to κ; the prevalence- and bias-adjusted kappa, PABAK $= 2p_o - 1$, is usually credited to them. [Gwet's AC1](https://doi.org/10.1348/000711006X126600) is an alternative coefficient that is more stable at extreme prevalence. The minimum honest report for a binary judge is the full 2×2 table, or equivalently $p_o$, each rater's "yes" rate, and κ. A judge that says "yes" more often than the experts do is lenient. That is a bias worth knowing about even when κ looks acceptable. Leniency is among the failure modes that [Thakur et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12624) found in LLM judges, and their judges with high percent agreement still assigned scores far from the human ones.

## The human-panel baseline

Agreement with a human is only interpretable next to agreement *between* humans. If two experts reach κ = 0.2 on the same items, a judge at 0.2 against one expert is as good a stand-in for "an expert" as a second expert is. A judge can legitimately score somewhat *above* the human–human figure: by the reliability cap above, a judge that tracked the experts' shared signal perfectly would correlate with one expert at about $\sqrt{r}$, where $r$ is the expert–expert correlation (on the correlation scale, not κ). Agreement beyond $\sqrt{r}$ has to come from something else the judge shares with that expert, such as a taste for polished prose, and deserves suspicion. Journal peer review averages κ ≈ 0.17 ([Patterns §2](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#2-the-ratings-you-collect-are-a-biased-sample)), so in judgment-bound domains this ceiling is low. It has to be measured per task, by having at least some items rated independently by two or more humans.

Aggregate figures also hide where agreement comes from. When many items have genuinely split human labels, a judge can match or beat human–human agreement with the majority label while falling well below it on the items humans agree on; stratifying the comparison by human disagreement exposes this ([Elangovan et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03775)). Forcing raters to pick one label on such items makes it worse: across 11 rating tasks, judges chosen by agreement with forced-choice labels performed up to 31% worse, by the authors' measure, than judges chosen against the set of ratings each rater considered reasonable ([Guerdan et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05965)). Where items admit more than one defensible label, collect every label each rater would accept.

Two details make the comparison fair:

- **Compare like with like.** A judge scored against a panel's majority vote is being compared with an aggregate that is less noisy than any single member. The matching human baseline is one held-out panelist against the rest of the panel, not panelist against panelist. The *alternative annotator test* formalizes this ([Calderon, Reichart & Dror 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10970)). It drops each human annotator in turn and asks whether the LLM agrees with the remaining annotators at least as well as the dropped human does. It allows the LLM a margin ε for being cheaper (0.2 against experts, 0.1 against crowd workers) and passes it if it beats at least half the annotators; the authors recommend at least three annotators and 50–100 items.
- **Measure per task, not per model.** The same judge can be reliable on one property and poor on another, and agreement measured on easy items does not transfer to hard ones ([evidence](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#what-the-judge-literature-measures)).

HealthBench's grader validation is a large-scale instance: on consensus rubric criteria graded by several physicians, the GPT-4.1 grader was scored against the physicians as each physician was scored against the others. Its macro-F1 beat the average physician's in five of seven themes and the 33rd percentile of physicians in all seven ([Arora et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)).

## Calibration

A judge that outputs a probability ("the panel would renew this with probability 0.7") gives more information per audited item than one that outputs a label, and its probabilities can be scored. Use a *strictly proper* scoring rule, one whose expected score is optimized only by reporting one's true belief: the Brier score (squared error) or the log score ([Gneiting & Raftery 2007](https://doi.org/10.1198/016214506000001437)). The Brier score decomposes into a *reliability* term (forecasters' name for calibration error, unrelated to the reliability above), a *resolution* term, which measures how much the forecasts separate items with different outcomes, and an uncertainty term fixed by the base rate ([Murphy 1973](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0450(1973)012%3C0595:ANVPOT%3E2.0.CO;2)). Plot calibration by binning items by stated probability and comparing each bin's mean to its observed rate. Resolution is what makes a calibrated judge useful rather than merely honest: a judge that says 0.8 for every item is perfectly calibrated at an 80% base rate and useless.

LLMs' verbalized confidences tend to be overconfident ([Xiong et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13063)), so a judge's raw probabilities should be recalibrated on audited items before use, and the calibration then checked on audited items not used to fit it. At audit scale, use Platt scaling: its two parameters beat isotonic regression on calibration sets below roughly 200–1,000 items ([Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana 2005](https://doi.org/10.1145/1102351.1102430)).

Calibration matters operationally because escalation rules run on it. "Send items below 70% confidence to a human" means something only if 70% means 70%. The sibling wiki's [calibration chapter](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/hardening-calibration/) covers the case where calibration must hold in the tail.

## Error bars and sample sizes

Every number above is an estimate from a sample of items, and the sample is usually small because labels are expensive. [Miller (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640) sets out the practice for LLM evals, and it applies unchanged to judges:

- treat the items as a draw from a larger population and report standard errors;
- cluster the standard errors when items come in related groups (several criteria from one document, several questions from one passage); in Miller's example clustered errors were up to three times the naive ones;
- compare two judges on the *same* items using paired differences;
- run a power analysis before collecting labels.

For a proportion near $p$, a 95% interval of half-width $h$ needs $n \approx 1.96^2\, p(1-p)/h^2$ items. That is 246 items for ±5 points at $p = 0.8$, and 62 for ±10. Kappa is far noisier than the proportion it is built from. With both raters at an 80% "yes" rate, a κ estimated from 50 items has a 95% sampling spread of about ±0.3 whether the true value is 0.17 or 0.4. At the true κ ≈ 0.17 typical of peer review, about 300 double-rated items are needed for 80% power to distinguish the judge from chance with the standard test of κ = 0. These figures come from simulating the 2×2 table and are reproduced in the [worked example](/concepts/worked-example/#what-50-audits-buy). Bootstrap the interval for κ or α rather than trusting a normal approximation at these sizes.

## Prediction-powered inference

The audit design in [LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-design-pattern-llms-as-the-cheap-layer) produces two datasets: the judge's score $f$ on all $N$ items, and gold labels $y$ on a random $n$ of them. The naive estimator of a population quantity, such as the share of grants experts would renew, uses only the $n$ gold labels. Plugging in the judge's scores on all $N$ items is precise but biased by however wrong the judge is. Prediction-powered inference (PPI) uses both. It takes the judge's average over all $N$ items and corrects it by the judge's average error on the $n$ audited ones:

$$\hat\theta_{\text{PP}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i \;-\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} (f_j - y_j)$$

The result is unbiased whatever the judge's quality, provided the audited items are a uniformly random draw (or have known inclusion probabilities) and the judge is frozen before the audit labels are seen. Its variance is roughly $\mathrm{Var}(f)/N + \mathrm{Var}(f - y)/n$, so the interval narrows as the judge's errors shrink ([Angelopoulos et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.09633)). PPI++ adds a tuning weight on $f$, chosen from the data, so that, asymptotically, the interval is never wider than the gold-labels-only one ([Angelopoulos, Duchi & Zrnic 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01453)). Several refinements fit audit design directly:

- **Stratification.** Stratified PPI helps when the judge is better on some kinds of item than others ([Fisch et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04291)). This is also the principled form of "oversample near the decision boundary, then reweight".
- **Active selection.** Active inference spends the label budget on the items where the model is least certain, while keeping valid intervals ([Zrnic & Candès 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03208)).
- **Model evaluation.** Applied to evaluating ML models with GPT-4 labels, these methods raised the effective human-labelled sample size by up to 50% ([Boyeau et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07008)).

The gain is easy to state for a mean. With $N \gg n$ and the PPI++ weight, the variance is the gold-only variance times $1 - \rho^2$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between the judge's score and the gold label, so $n$ audits are worth $n/(1-\rho^2)$ gold labels. Doubling them takes $\rho \approx 0.71$; a tenfold saving takes $\rho \approx 0.95$. When the judge is no more accurate than the model being evaluated, no debiasing method can cut the gold labels needed by more than half ([Dorner, Nastl & Hardt 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13341)), and in their experiments the savings were smaller. In the illustrative simulation below, the judge's score has $\rho \approx 0.74$ (κ ≈ 0.8 at a 0.5 threshold) and narrows the interval on the renewal rate by about 30%; a noisier judge with $\rho \approx 0.5$ (κ ≈ 0.4) narrows it by about an eighth. PPI makes a weak judge *safe* to use, because the estimate stays valid; it does not make a weak judge *useful*.

```python

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def kappa(a, b):
    """Cohen's kappa for two raters' labels on the same items."""
    po = np.mean(a == b)
    pe = sum(np.mean(a == k) * np.mean(b == k) for k in np.union1d(a, b))
    return (po - pe) / (1 - pe)

def bootstrap_ci(a, b, stat=kappa, reps=5000):
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(a), (reps, len(a)))
    return np.nanpercentile([stat(a[i], b[i]) for i in idx], [2.5, 97.5])

def n_for_halfwidth(p, h, z=1.96):
    """Items needed for a 95% interval of +/-h on a proportion near p."""
    return int(np.ceil(z**2 * p * (1 - p) / h**2))

def ppi_mean(y_lab, f_lab, f_all, z=1.96):
    """PPI++ estimate of mean(y): model scores f on all N items, gold y on n."""
    n, N = len(y_lab), len(f_all)
    lam = np.cov(y_lab, f_lab)[0, 1] / ((1 + n / N) * f_lab.var(ddof=1))
    est = lam * f_all.mean() + (y_lab - lam * f_lab).mean()
    se = np.sqrt(lam**2 * f_all.var(ddof=1) / N + (y_lab - lam * f_lab).var(ddof=1) / n)
    return est, est - z * se, est + z * se

# Illustrative population: 1,000 items, experts say "yes" to 80%;
# the model outputs a probability that is informative but noisy.
N, n = 1000, 50
y = rng.random(N) < 0.8
f = np.clip(np.where(y, 0.75, 0.35) + rng.normal(0, 0.15, N), 0, 1)
lab = rng.choice(N, n, replace=False)          # the random audit
y_lab, f_lab = y[lab].astype(float), f[lab]

print("kappa (model at 0.5 vs expert):", round(kappa(f_lab > 0.5, y[lab]), 2),
      "95% CI", np.round(bootstrap_ci(f_lab > 0.5, y[lab]), 2))
m, se = y_lab.mean(), np.sqrt(y_lab.var(ddof=1) / n)
print("audit only:", np.round([m, m - 1.96 * se, m + 1.96 * se], 3))
print("PPI++     :", np.round(ppi_mean(y_lab, f_lab, f), 3))
print("audits for +/-5 points at 80%:", n_for_halfwidth(0.8, 0.05))
```

Output (NumPy 2.5):

```
kappa (model at 0.5 vs expert): 0.82 95% CI [0.56 1.  ]
audit only: [0.8   0.688 0.912]
PPI++     : [0.791 0.712 0.87 ]
audits for +/-5 points at 80%: 246
```

Over 2,000 repetitions of this simulated audit, the gold-only and PPI++ intervals covered the true renewal rate 93% and 94% of the time, near the nominal 95%. Their average widths were 0.22 and 0.15. Note the bootstrap interval on κ: even for a strong judge, 50 items pin κ down only to somewhere between "moderate" and "near perfect".

## Gaming tests

Every measurement above is taken at zero optimization pressure. A judge that will gate anything of value should also be measured against inputs built to fool it, and the attacks in the literature double as a test suite. The evidence for each is in [LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#evidence-under-optimization-pressure); the tests are:

| Test | What it measures | Pass condition |
|---|---|---|
| **Null model.** Submit a constant response unrelated to the instruction, including crafted ones ([Zheng et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07137)) | whether the judge can be won without doing the task | null submissions score at the floor |
| **Master keys.** Append generic openers or symbols ("Thought process:", ":") to wrong answers ([Zhao et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08794)), and universal adversarial phrases transferred from a surrogate model ([Raina, Liusie & Gales 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14016)) | false-positive rate on known-bad inputs | false positives no higher than on unmodified bad inputs |
| **Injection.** Embed instructions to the judge in the evaluated text, as found in 2025 arXiv preprints aimed at AI reviewers | whether evaluated content can instruct the evaluator | verdict unchanged by the injected text |
| **Swaps and padding.** Reverse answer order, add length without content | position and verbosity bias | verdict invariant to order; score not increased by padding |
| **Best-of-n pressure.** Have a model rewrite each test item $n$ ways, keep the judge's favourite, and have experts grade originals and winners blind | how far judge score and expert grade diverge under selection, the curve [Gao, Schulman & Hilton (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760) measured for reward models | the winners' expert grade rises with the judge's score, or at least does not fall, as $n$ grows |
| **Selective disclosure.** Let one party submit many private variants and keep the best | the *process*, not the judge: best-of-k inflates scores even against an honest judge ([Singh et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879)) | variants are counted, or all scores published |

Report each result with an error bar, as for any other measurement. Re-run the suite whenever the judge's model or prompt changes. Passing it is necessary, not sufficient: these are the *known* attacks, and an evaluated party with query access can search for new ones. The best-of-$n$ test simulates that search only at small $n$. Only random audits with a penalty for detected gaming address unknown attacks ([LLMs as Evaluators, step 3](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-design-pattern-llms-as-the-cheap-layer)).

## What to report

For any evaluator, human or model, before its scores are used: the task and population it was measured on; its self-agreement under re-runs or fuzzed prompts; its chance-corrected agreement with humans, with the confusion table and each rater's base rate; the human–human agreement on the same items, with the same statistic; bootstrap intervals on all of these; its calibration, if it outputs probabilities; its results on the gaming tests; and the date and model version, since every one of these numbers expires when either changes.

## Open questions

- How small can the double-rated set be in practice, given that the human–human baseline has the same sampling error as the judge–human number it is compared to?
- PPI is unbiased for what the panel would say, panel noise included. When the target is the latent quality the panel measures badly (κ ≈ 0.2), what estimator, or what second source of signal, recovers it?
- Does a judge's best-of-$n$ curve at small $n$ predict how fast it degrades when real evaluated parties optimize against it for months?


------------------------------------------------------------
## Interlude: A Worked Example
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/worked-example/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: early draft, September 2026; agreement analysis corrected October 2026, and the statistics follow [Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/). **Every cost and rate assumed on this page is illustrative**, chosen to be round and plausible, not measured, and no ranking of designs rests on them. They are stated so each can be swapped for a real figure. The point is the shape of the trade-off, and which design questions become quantitative once you write the numbers down. This page answers the most-repeated request in [external commentary](/reference/objections/#external-commentary): a concrete, even fictional, case showing what better evaluation buys.*

## The problem

A funder makes or renews about **1,000 grants a year** and wants each one evaluated after a year: did it deliver roughly what it promised, and should it be renewed? Today the funder does what most do. A few program officers read the reports they have time for, and most grants get renewed on momentum.

**Assumptions** (all illustrative; swap in real numbers):

| Quantity | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Expert review of one grant | one reviewer, 4 hours at \$150/hour = **\$600** | a careful read of the report, outputs, and a call. A three-person panel would cost \$1,800 |
| LLM evaluation, marginal | **\$1** per grant | several runs across prompts and models (opinion-fuzzed), not one call |
| LLM evaluation, fixed | **\$10,000–30,000** a year | rubric design, a calibration set, engineering, re-validation after model updates. The sibling wiki's [study of QURI's deployments](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/case-studies/llm-epistemics-in-production/) calls prompt engineering "a recurring tax, not a setup cost" |
| Share of grants an expert would renew | **80%** | "renewed on momentum" suggests a high rate |
| Agreement between two experts reviewing the same grant | **unknown** | has to be measured. Journal peer review averages κ ≈ 0.17 ([Patterns §2](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#2-the-ratings-you-collect-are-a-biased-sample)). In a replicated NIH study section, reviewers of 25 applications showed no agreement (Krippendorff's α = 0.02), though all 25 were eventually funded, which restricts the range ([Pier et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1714379115)). Ex-post renewal may differ |

## Four designs

| Design | What runs | Annual cost | Grants an expert sees | What you learn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Artisanal, full** | experts review all 1,000 | \$600,000 | 1,000 | the best available judgment on everything, at a price few funders pay |
| **A′. Artisanal, what actually happens** | experts review the 100 they get to | \$60,000 | 100 | expert judgment on 10%; nothing on the other 900; no estimate of what was missed |
| **B. LLM only** | the model scores all 1,000 | \$11,000–31,000 | 0 | a score on everything, and *no idea how good the scores are* |
| **C. Prediction–evaluation** | the model scores all 1,000; a hidden random 50 get two independent expert reviews each | \$71,000–91,000 in year one | 50 | a score on everything **plus a measured agreement rate**, against a measured expert–expert baseline |
| **D. C + escalation** | as C, plus one expert review of the ~100 grants where the model's runs disagree most | \$131,000–151,000 | ~150 | as C, with expert judgment concentrated where the model is least sure |

C's cost is the model (\$1,000), its fixed cost, 50 audit reviews (\$30,000), and 50 second reviews to measure how often two experts agree (\$30,000); without annual second reviews it falls to \$41,000–61,000. So C costs somewhat more than A′ in year one and about the same or less later, while covering ten times as many grants. That comparison turns on the fixed cost and the price of expert time, so it is not a finding. What does not depend on the numbers: only C and D measure their own error rate, and B's low price buys scores of unknown worth.

## What 50 audits buy

The audit estimates how often the model's renew/don't call matches the expert's. Because the 50 are drawn at random, the sample agreement rate is an unbiased estimate of agreement across all 1,000. Its 95% interval is about ±11 points at 80% agreement (binomial, $1.96\sqrt{a(1-a)/n}$), ±8 points with 100 audits, and ±5.5 with 200.

Raw agreement is the wrong scale, though. If the expert renews 80% of grants, a model that renews 80% at random agrees with the expert $0.8^2 + 0.2^2 = 68\%$ of the time. Cohen's $\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)$ rescales observed agreement $p_o$ so that chance agreement $p_e$ scores 0 and perfect agreement 1 ([Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#agreement-corrected-for-chance), which also covers the prevalence paradox at work here):

| | expert renews 50% | expert renews 80% |
|---|---|---|
| chance agreement $p_e$ | 50% | 68% |
| raw agreement at κ = 0.17 | 58.5% | 73% |
| raw agreement at κ = 0.4 | 70% | 81% |
| κ implied by 70% raw agreement | 0.40 | 0.06 |

An earlier version of this page assumed experts agree "about 70%" of the time. At an 80% renewal rate that is barely better than chance. The audit report should therefore give the 2×2 table and both raters' renewal rates, not one agreement figure; a model that renews 90% where experts renew 80% is lenient even if its κ looks acceptable.

Precision is the second problem. In simulation (both raters renewing 80% of grants), a κ estimated from 50 audits has a 95% interval of about ±0.3. A model whose true κ against the expert is 0.17 gets an interval excluding zero in only 12–26% of 50-audit samples, depending on the test; 80% power takes about 300 audits with the standard test of κ = 0, more with a Wald interval. At κ = 0.4, power is about 60–78% with 50 audits and 86–96% with 100. Where expert agreement is as weak as in journal peer review, 50 audits cannot tell a model that matches the experts from one that is guessing.

The comparison that matters is model–expert κ against expert–expert κ. If two experts reach κ = 0.17 on the same grants, a model at 0.17 is as good a stand-in for "an expert" as a second expert. Design C's second reviews measure the expert–expert number, which carries the same sampling error. With two experts per grant, the fair comparison is model vs. expert A against expert B vs. expert A. A formal test of whether the model can replace an expert, the alternative annotator test, needs at least three experts per item ([Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#the-human-panel-baseline)).

Two ways to get more out of each audit:

- **Score probabilities, not matches.** Have the model output the probability that the expert renews, and score it with a proper scoring rule such as Brier or log loss ([calibration](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#calibration)). This uses the model's confidence instead of discarding it at a threshold.
- **Estimate the population, not just agreement.** Prediction-powered inference ([Angelopoulos et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.09633)) combines the model's scores on all 1,000 grants with the 50 audits to give a confidence interval for the expert-judged renewal rate. The interval is valid whatever the model's quality. How much it narrows depends on the model. In the chapter's [simulation](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#prediction-powered-inference), with illustrative numbers, a model at κ ≈ 0.8 against the expert shrinks the 50-audit interval from about ±11 to ±7.5 points, worth roughly doubling the audits. A model at κ ≈ 0.4 shrinks it by about an eighth. This is a portfolio estimate (what share of grants experts would renew); it does not make any single renewal decision more accurate.

## Three refinements, and their prices

**Audit the decision boundary, then reweight.** The average agreement rate hides where errors fall. Errors among clear renewals and clear rejections cost little; errors near the funding threshold cost the most. Oversampling audits near the threshold spends the expert budget where it matters. It breaks the simple estimator, though: the sample is no longer uniform, so each audited item must be weighted by the inverse of its probability of being selected (the Horvitz–Thompson estimator) to keep the overall estimate unbiased. Stratify, but record the sampling probabilities; stratified PPI combines this with the model scores ([Fisch et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04291)).

**Assume applicants will learn the model.** Once grantees know a model reads their reports, they write for the model. This is [Goodhart](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#1-the-measure-reshapes-the-measured), and it arrives on the second cycle, not the first; reviewing is already [being targeted](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#evidence-under-optimization-pressure). Running the known [gaming tests](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#gaming-tests) before launch removes the cheapest exploits, not the incentive. The random audit *detects* this: agreement tracked round over round is the drift alarm, and a falling rate means the model is being gamed or the population has shifted. Either way, stop trusting the layer until it is re-validated. Given the precision above, a 50-item audit will only catch a large drop. Detection alone doesn't *deter*, though. That takes a consequence when an audit exposes a report written for the model (for example, the grant is re-reviewed in full and the gaming noted in the grantee's file), and it helps not to publish the model or prompt.

**Escalate on disagreement, not on score.** Design D sends experts the items where the model's own runs (across prompts and models) disagree most. Those are the items where the cheap layer is least reliable, so expert time buys the most there. Escalated items are chosen non-randomly, so they must not be pooled into the agreement estimate; only the random 50 measure the model's accuracy. Escalating at random with probability rising with disagreement, and recording the probabilities, would let those reviews count too ([active inference](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#prediction-powered-inference)).

## What the example leaves out

- **Value.** The table prices evaluation but not what it is worth. That requires knowing how many renewal decisions would change, and how much the changed decisions improve outcomes: a value-of-information estimate ([Cruxes](/start-here/key-questions/#on-bridging-cheap-and-expensive-judgment), question 9). The sibling wiki's [Core Model](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/core-model/) sketches how to price information; this page does not apply it, so nothing here says whether any design is worth its cost.
- **Trust.** Grantees and the funder's board have to accept model-scored renewals. An audited error rate helps, but [epistemic culture](/concepts/epistemic-culture/) decides whether a published "the model agreed with experts as often as experts agree with each other (κ ≈ 0.2)" reads as reassurance or as an admission.
- **Correlated error.** If the model and the expert share a blind spot (both favor polished reports, say), agreement overstates accuracy. The audit measures agreement with experts, not with the truth.

## Try it with real numbers

Each assumption above can be replaced with a measured figure from one funder's records: hours per review, the fraction of grants actually reviewed, the renewal rate, and, most usefully, the chance-corrected agreement between two officers who review the same grant independently. A funder willing to run design C for one cycle would produce the first real data point this page asks for. If the officers' agreement turns out low, the audit has to be several times larger than 50.


------------------------------------------------------------
## 11. The Capability Ladder
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/capability-ladder/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft v0, October 2026. The rungs are this wiki's proposal. The placements are judgments from public documentation and will be wrong wherever a system measures more internally than it publishes.*

Driving automation has graded levels, and laboratories and educational tests have standards ([below](#what-the-grading-suggests)); judgment-based evaluation in general has no shared way to say how far a system has got. This page proposes one. Each rung is defined by something the system must be able to measure or do, so a grade can be checked rather than asserted. The unit being graded is the standing system, not a single evaluation ([Evaluation as a System](/concepts/the-systems-view/)).

## The rungs

| Rung | Name | The system can… | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Ad hoc | produce judgments | none: each judgment is made its own way |
| 1 | Standardized | apply one written procedure and output scale to every item, and keep records | two items judged a year apart sit on the same scale and trace to the rubric version used |
| 2 | Measured | state its error on a defined population, with an interval | it publishes chance-corrected agreement with independent raters, alongside the rater–rater baseline, or a proper-score track record against resolved outcomes |
| 3 | Monitored | re-measure that error in operation and notice when it moves | a standing audit stream on random or hidden items; every accuracy figure carries a date and version; re-validation triggers are declared in advance |
| 4 | Gaming-tested | state its error under deliberate attempts to fool it | an attack suite or red team has been run against it, success rates are reported, and detected gaming is penalized |
| 5 | Accountable | be checked and contested by parties it does not control | independent audit of the whole system; disclosed payer and conflicts; an appeal route for the evaluated whose outcomes feed back into measurement |

A system's grade is the highest rung whose test it passes together with every rung below. The ordering is a claim about dependence: drift (3) cannot be detected without a measured baseline (2), and the cost of an attack (4) cannot be stated without the unattacked error. Rung 5 is institutional rather than technical, and real systems often acquire it out of order. A jagged profile is information, not a grading error: credit ratings now have strong external oversight but failed under issuer pressure. "Error" at rungs 2–4 means disagreement with a reference (raters or resolved outcomes), which is validity only to the extent that the reference is what the system is meant to track ([Reliability is not validity](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#reliability-is-not-validity)).

The ladder does not grade whether the question is worth asking, or cost. A rung-4 system can be too expensive to run ([the design space](/concepts/the-systems-view/#the-design-space)). The methods behind rungs 2–4 are in [Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/); the operational steps are in the [Launch Checklist](/concepts/launch-checklist/).

## Eight systems graded

✓ passes, ~ partial, ✗ fails or absent, ? not publicly documented.

| System | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | Grade |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Journal and grant peer review | ✓ | ~ | ✗ | ✗ | ~ | 1 |
| Cochrane systematic reviews | ✓ | ~ | ? | ? | ~ | 1 |
| Credit ratings (US NRSROs) | ✓ | ✓ | ~ | ✗ | ✓ | 2 |
| LMArena | ✓ | ✓ | ? | ~ | ~ | 2 |
| Community Notes (X) | ✓ | ~ | ? | ✓ | ~ | 1–2 |
| METR capability evaluations | ✓ | ✓ | ? | ~ | ~ | 2–3 |
| Metaculus | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ? | ~ | 3 |
| GRE essay scoring (e-rater plus human) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ~ | 4 |

**Peer review.** Journals and funders use fixed criteria and score scales, but reliability is mostly measured by outside researchers. A meta-analysis of 48 studies found mean inter-rater κ ≈ 0.17 ([Bornmann, Mutz & Daniel 2010](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0014331)). In a mock NIH study section, 43 reviewers scoring the same 25 funded oncology applications showed little agreement in scores or written critiques ([Pier et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1714379115)). The partial mark is for NeurIPS, which sent 10% of submissions to two independent committees in 2014 and again in 2021; both times about half the accepted list would have changed on a rerun ([Beygelzimer et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03262)). Gaming tests come from outside, as stings: a fabricated paper with obvious flaws was accepted by 157 of 304 open-access journals, with no subscription journals tested ([Bohannon 2013](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.342.6154.60)), and hidden prompts aimed at AI reviewers ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#evidence-under-optimization-pressure)) show a newer exposure.

**Cochrane.** The Handbook and the RoB 2 risk-of-bias tool standardize the procedure. Their reliability is again measured externally, and poorly: four experienced raters applying RoB 2 to 70 trials reached Fleiss' κ 0.16 on the overall judgment, at about 28 minutes per outcome ([Minozzi et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2020.06.015)). Cochrane's strength is institutional: commercial organizations with a financial interest in a review's outcome may not fund it ([commercial sponsorship policy](https://www.cochrane.org/learn/resources/commercial-sponsorship-policy)). Grade 1 with rung-5 features, which is the opposite profile to credit ratings.

**Credit ratings.** Registered agencies must publish standardized performance statistics (transition and default rates) as Exhibit 1 to Form NRSRO, and SEC staff must examine each agency at least annually ([SEC Office of Credit Ratings staff report, Jan. 2025](https://www.sec.gov/files/jan-2025-ocr-staff-report.pdf)). That is rungs 2 and 5. Rung 4 failed in practice: the official inquiry called the agencies' failures "essential cogs in the wheel of financial destruction" ([FCIC 2011](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-FCIC/pdf/GPO-FCIC.pdf)). Most of the examination regime postdates the failure, and nobody has shown that it tests resistance to issuer pressure rather than compliance.

**LMArena.** Pairwise votes, a Bradley–Terry model and published confidence intervals give rungs 1–2. Its builders checked crowd votes against expert raters and found good agreement ([Chiang et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04132)). Rung 4 is split. Vote manipulation was tested with the operators: in an offline simulation about a thousand votes could move a target model's rank, and mitigations were deployed ([Huang et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07493)). The process failed: a few providers tested many private variants and published only the best ([Singh et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879)).

**Community Notes.** The bridging algorithm and the rating data are public so that outsiders can audit them ([X help centre](https://help.x.com/en/using-x/community-notes)). Its developers validated note selection with a survey experiment and a reshare effect in deployment ([Wojcik et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.15723)), but no routine error rate on a random sample of displayed notes has been published. Rung 4 has a recent pass of the useful kind: a study co-authored with the Community Notes team found that up to 10.7% of lower-quality notes in historical data could be pushed over the display threshold with fewer than 10 coordinated ratings, and mitigations were deployed ([Selvam et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01824)). An independent simulation found 5–20% bad raters could suppress targeted helpful notes ([Truong et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02615)). The profile is the reverse of most systems': attacked and patched before its unattacked error is measured.

**METR.** Task suites with timed human baselines, and capability estimates with hierarchical-bootstrap 95% intervals ([Kwa et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499)), give rungs 1–2. Here the evaluated party is the model, and it can game in either direction. METR checks for inflation: o3 reward-hacked in 30.4% of RE-Bench runs and 0.7% of HCAST runs, and successful hacks are excluded from reported results, though METR says it may miss some ([METR 2025](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking)). For a dangerous-capability evaluation the worse direction is deflation. Models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform selectively on such evaluations ([van der Weij et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07358)), and frontier models tell evaluation transcripts from deployment well above chance ([Needham et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23836)). METR's GPT-5 report found no significant evidence of sandbagging but noted that its monitors miss many misbehaviours and that a capable enough model could evade them ([METR, Aug. 2025](https://metr.org/evaluations/gpt-5-report/)). That is a partial pass on rung 4. Whether error is re-measured across releases in a way that would meet rung 3 is not documented publicly, hence the range.

**Metaculus.** Every resolved question is scored with proper scoring rules, and the platform publishes a [track record](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/track-record/) with calibration curves. Because most questions resolve (some are annulled), the audit stream is nearly the whole population rather than a sample. We know of no published test of how the community forecast responds to deliberate manipulation.

**GRE essay scoring.** Each Analytical Writing essay is scored by a trained human reader and by e-rater; if they disagree, a second human scores it and the human scores are averaged ([ETS](https://www.ets.org/gre/test-takers/general-test/transcript/preparing-for-the-analytical-writing-measure.html)). ETS published machine–human agreement for the GRE prompts ([Ramineni et al. 2012](https://www.ets.org/research/policy_research_reports/publications/report/2012/jdyu.html)), including by subgroup: e-rater matched human raters for most groups but scored essays from mainland China much higher ([Bridgeman, Trapani & Attali 2012](https://doi.org/10.1080/08957347.2012.635502)). The engine alone fails gaming tests. Outsiders invited by ETS to fool it inflated scores more often than they deflated them, and the authors concluded it should not be the sole scorer in high-stakes use ([Powers et al. 2002](https://www.ets.org/research/policy_research_reports/publications/article/2002/cnrp.html)); later, gibberish from the BABEL generator got the top score in 16 of 38 submissions to ETS's practice service ([Perelman 2020](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/263565cq)). The system passes rung 4 because a human reads every essay and an off-topic essay scores zero; test takers can pay for a [score review](https://ets.org/content/dam/ets-org/pdfs/gre/gre-score-review-request-form.pdf), a partial rung 5. The top grade thus goes to a design in which the machine checks a human on every item and saves at most the second read: evidence that the [cheap layer](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-design-pattern-llms-as-the-cheap-layer) can check, not that the human can be removed.

## What the grading suggests

These are eight hand-picked systems, so the observations are hypotheses. The most trusted systems by reputation (peer review, Cochrane) grade lowest on measurement, which suggests trust tracks institutional standing more than measured error. The highest grades go to systems whose reference arrives cheaply (questions resolve; a human reads every essay). The top grade also goes to the one system built under a mature measurement standard: educational testing's [*Standards*](https://www.testingstandards.net/open-access-files.html) (AERA, APA & NCME 2014) require validity and reliability evidence, quality control of scoring, and a route for test takers to challenge results. [ISO/IEC 17025](https://webstore.iec.ch/publication/62135) does the same for testing laboratories: accredited labs must evaluate measurement uncertainty and monitor the validity of results, including by proficiency testing against other labs where available ([clauses 7.6–7.7](https://www.pjlabs.com/understanding-iso-iec-17025-clauses-7-6-and-7-7)), under independent accreditation. Other fields can borrow these rather than start from scratch. And every system that has been seriously attacked, whether by issuers, model providers, coordinated raters or the model itself, was attacked through the incentive the score created. That is the [Goodhart pattern](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#1-the-measure-reshapes-the-measured), and it is why rung 4 cannot be skipped by anything that gates value.

The sibling RRP wiki's [Reliability Ladder](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/epistemic-applications/) grades *applications* of strong reasoners by how much verified trust they need; mapping its tiers to these rungs is open work.

## Open questions

- Do the rungs discriminate? Grading the [161 catalogue systems](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/#does-who-pays-predict-failure) would show whether most cluster at 1, and whether grade predicts documented failure better than [funding model](/concepts/the-systems-view/#technical-and-institutional-design-variables) does.
- Should rung 5 be a separate axis rather than a rung? The Cochrane and credit-rating profiles argue for two axes, technical and institutional.
- What is the minimal rung-4 evidence for a judge facing unknown attacks, given that a suite only covers known ones?


------------------------------------------------------------
## 12. Launch Checklist
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/launch-checklist/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, October 2026. A checklist, not an argument; the reasons are on the linked pages. Items 5–8 and 13 correspond to rungs 2–3 of the [capability ladder](/concepts/capability-ladder/), items 9 and 14 to rung 4, and items 2, 11, 15 and 16 to rung 5.*

Written for a system with a cheap evaluator (an LLM, a crowd, junior raters) standing in for an expensive one (an expert panel). Most items apply to any evaluation system.

## Before building

1. **Name the decision.** Which decision the score feeds, who acts on it, and what an error costs in each direction. If no decision changes, stop. ([Design space](/concepts/the-systems-view/#the-design-space))
2. **Fix the payer and the metric owner.** Write down who funds the system, who can change the rubric, and every conflict of interest; publish them. In this wiki's hand-coded catalogue, systems paid by the rated party had about 3.5 times the odds of a documented failure, though whether payment or high stakes drives that is unresolved. ([Catalogue coding](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/#does-who-pays-predict-failure))
3. **Budget the expensive layer as a recurring cost.** Audits, re-validation and the reference panel run for the life of the system, not once at setup. ([Worked example](/concepts/worked-example/))
4. **Version the rubric.** Every score records the rubric, prompt and model version that produced it.

## Before trusting a score

5. **Measure the human baseline.** Double-rate a calibration set with independent experts and report chance-corrected agreement (κ, AC1 or α) with each rater's base rate. Without this number, the cheap evaluator's agreement cannot be interpreted. Write down what the panel stands in for, and where real outcomes later arrive, score panel and model against them: agreement with a panel is no more valid than the panel. ([Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#the-human-panel-baseline); [reliability is not validity](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#reliability-is-not-validity))
6. **Measure the cheap evaluator against it.** Use the same statistic, against a held-out panelist rather than the panel consensus, with bootstrap intervals, on items not used to write or tune the prompt; check calibration if it outputs probabilities. Measure separately on the hard items near the decision threshold, and on each group the decision must treat fairly: e-rater scored essays from mainland China much higher than human raters did ([Bridgeman, Trapani & Attali 2012](https://doi.org/10.1080/08957347.2012.635502)). ([Measuring an Evaluator](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#agreement-corrected-for-chance))
7. **Set kill criteria in advance.** The agreement or false-positive rate below which the system stops issuing scores. Automated essay scoring offers a precedent: machine–human weighted κ no more than 0.10 below human–human ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#what-the-judge-literature-measures)).

## Before launch

8. **Plan the audit.** A hidden random sample of live items goes to the expensive evaluator; size it to detect a breach of the kill criteria ([power](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#error-bars-and-sample-sizes)), and estimate population quantities with prediction-powered inference rather than raw model output ([PPI](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#prediction-powered-inference)). Auditors must not see the cheap evaluator's score: people shown automated advice tend to follow it when it is wrong ([Goddard, Roudsari & Wyatt 2012](https://doi.org/10.1136/amiajnl-2011-000089)).
9. **Run the gaming tests.** Null responses, injected instructions, padding, order swaps, and best-of-k submission, each with a false-positive rate and an interval. Attach a penalty to gaming that an audit detects; audits without one measure gaming but do not deter it. ([Gaming tests](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#gaming-tests); [LLMs as Evaluators, step 3](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-design-pattern-llms-as-the-cheap-layer))
10. **Write the escalation rule.** Low confidence or disagreement across prompts or models sends an item to the expensive layer. Assume the rule will become known; escalation catches honest uncertainty, not attacks. ([Trust or Escalate](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-design-pattern-llms-as-the-cheap-layer))
11. **Open an appeal route.** The evaluated party can contest a score and get human review. Count appeal outcomes as non-random audits: they show where the system errs against those who complain, not the error rate. In the EU this is partly law: where solely automated decisions about people are allowed at all, the GDPR gives them a right to human intervention and to contest the decision ([Art. 22(3)](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-22-gdpr/)), and AI that evaluates learners, job candidates or creditworthiness is high-risk under the AI Act from December 2027 ([Epistemic Culture](/concepts/epistemic-culture/#rollout)).
12. **Check incentives for the raters.** If predictors or raters are paid only on audited items, a proper score stays proper, but the incentive to spend effort on any one item shrinks with the audit fraction: 1 in 200 at 50 of 10,000. ([Techniques](/concepts/techniques/#predictionevaluation-systems))

## While running

13. **Monitor drift.** Track audit agreement over time with a control chart or sequential test rather than a fresh significance test at each look, and track the expensive raters' agreement with each other, since the reference drifts too. Re-validate on any new model or prompt version, any change in the evaluated population, and any rise in the stakes attached to the score. ([Two system-level failures](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-two-system-level-failures))
14. **Re-run the gaming suite** on every re-validation, and add attacks found in the wild.
15. **Publish the report card.** Task and population, self-agreement, chance-corrected agreement with the human baseline, calibration, gaming false-positive rates, audit results, and the date and version of each. ([What to report](/concepts/measuring-an-evaluator/#what-to-report))
16. **Invite outside audit.** Give an independent party the audit data and, where possible, the rubric and model. Credit ratings show an external examiner is necessary but not sufficient. ([Capability ladder](/concepts/capability-ladder/#eight-systems-graded))


================================================================================
# Part III — Evidence from the Wild
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## 13. Evaluation Systems in the Wild
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: curated catalogue, assembled from a June 2026 sweep; coded by payer, method and documented failure in October 2026 ([below](#does-who-pays-predict-failure)). This is the descriptive companion to the conceptual pages: the world is already full of standing systems that produce many evaluations of a repeated type. They are the field's case record: its documented successes, failures and capture stories. The founding program called for exactly this survey (the proto "process catalogue").*

A working catalogue, not a reference. Systems and links are verified, but **exact figures (coverage counts, market shares, percentages) are approximate and should be checked against the source** before relying on them. Where a number is load-bearing, follow the link.

## How to read this

Every entry names **what it evaluates**, its **output format**, its **method**, and one **notable weakness or failure**. Before the catalogue, four cross-cutting lenses that the systems below keep illustrating:

**Method archetypes.** Independent lab testing · professional anonymous inspection · expert panel/committee · critic aggregation · crowd reviews (often Bayesian/credibility-weighted) · two-sided/reciprocal rating · statistical/algorithmic model · composite index · market-based · regulatory review. These are the menu on [Evaluation Methods](/concepts/evaluation-methods/), seen in the wild.

**Output formats.** Stars (1–5), points (0–100), letter grades (A–F, AAA–D), rankings, pass/fail certification, tiers, probabilities, and dollar estimates. The format is an editorial choice with consequences — binary "fresh/rotten" discards intensity; 100-point wine scales compress to 88–100.

**Who pays.** Three funding archetypes recur:
1. **Independent / nonprofit, buys its own units, no ads** (Consumer Reports, Which?, Stiftung Warentest, IIHS). Even here, Which? and Stiftung Warentest sell logo licences to makers whose products score well.
2. **Affiliate / ad-funded editorial** (Wirecutter, RTINGS, CNET) — recommendation-revenue conflict.
3. **Rated party pays** — issuer-pays ratings, fee-for-certification, award-licensing (Moody's/S&P, UL, ISO, LEED, J.D. Power, DXOMARK).

How much this matters is tested [below](#does-who-pays-predict-failure); the answer is weaker than the hand-picked contrasts suggested.

**Recurring failure modes.** Fake reviews / astroturfing / review bombing · gaming and Goodharting (citations, ratings) · capture (credit ratings in 2008; the World Bank's *Doing Business* scandal) · pay-to-play · grade inflation · self-declaration abuse · snapshot-in-time validity · reciprocal retaliation in two-sided systems · opaque weighting.

---

## Consumer products & testing

- **[Consumer Reports](https://www.consumerreports.org/)** — consumer products & services. 0–100 scores + "Recommended"/"Best Buy". Independent lab testing + member reliability surveys; nonprofit, buys all units at retail, no ads. *Weakness:* affiliate-link revenue creates a perceived conflict.
- **[Which?](https://www.which.co.uk/)** (UK) — products & services. Scores + "Best Buy"/"Don't Buy". Independent lab testing; nonprofit.
- **[Stiftung Warentest](https://www.test.de/)** (Germany) — products & services. German school-grade scale, printed on packaging. Undercover purchasing + outsourced scientific testing; ad-free, government-seeded foundation. *Weakness:* sued by manufacturers ~10×/year.
- **[CHOICE](https://www.choice.com.au/)** (Australia) — products & services. Scores + "CHOICE Recommended". Accredited in-house labs; nonprofit.
- **[Wirecutter](https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/)** (NYT) — consumer gear. Narrative "top pick"/"budget pick", no scores. Hands-on reviewer testing; affiliate revenue, no on-site ads.
- **[RTINGS](https://www.rtings.com/)** — TVs, monitors, headphones, etc. 0–100 overall + per-use-case scores. Standardized in-house bench measurements. *Weakness:* 2025 scoring overhaul drew backlash over weighting; since March 2026 full test results are [members-only](https://www.rtings.com/company/revamping-our-membership-program).
- **[DXOMARK](https://www.dxomark.com/)** — camera/phone image, audio, display. Open-scale scores + sub-scores. Lab + structured perceptual testing. *Weakness:* core conflict — sells consulting to the firms it scores.
- **[Tom's Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/)** / **[PCMag](https://www.pcmag.com/)** — PC components/devices. Stars + "Editors' Choice" + hierarchy charts. Standardized benchmarking labs; affiliate + ads.
- **[J.D. Power](https://www.jdpower.com/business)** — vehicle quality/satisfaction. PP100 (problems per 100) + segment awards. Large owner surveys. *Weakness:* clients are the automakers; winners license the awards to advertise.
- **[Kelley Blue Book](https://www.kbb.com/)** / **[Edmunds](https://www.edmunds.com/)** — vehicle valuation & reviews. Dollar values (TMV / Blue Book Value). Statistical models on transaction data. *Weakness:* dealer-referral revenue; values can diverge from actual sales.
- **[Robert Parker / Wine Advocate](https://www.robertparker.com/)**, **[Wine Spectator](https://www.winespectator.com/)** — wine. 100-point scale. Professional critics, often blind. *Weakness:* "Parker palate" homogenization; score compression into 88–100.
- **[Untappd](https://untappd.com/)**, **[BeerAdvocate](https://www.beeradvocate.com/)**, **[RateBeer](https://www.ratebeer.com/)** — beer. Crowd star/score averages. *Weakness:* hype/novelty bias; RateBeer is owned by AB InBev (BeerAdvocate/Untappd by Next Glass) — big-brewer ownership of the rater.
- **[Coffee Review](https://www.coffeereview.com/)** — coffee. 100-point scale. Expert blind cupping. *Weakness:* pay-to-submit service; mostly 90+ published.
- **[America's Test Kitchen / Cook's Illustrated](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/)** — kitchen gear, ingredients, recipes. Tiered verdicts. Expert panels, blind taste tests, heavy repeated testing; no ads.

## Media, entertainment & content

- **[IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/)** — films, TV, people. 1–10 Bayesian-weighted average; "Top 250". Crowd votes. *Weakness:* vote brigading; demographic skew; polarized 1/10 voting.
- **[Rotten Tomatoes](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/)** — film/TV. % "fresh" critics + audience score. Binary critic aggregation (discards intensity). *Weakness:* review bombing of audience scores; binary loses nuance.
- **[Metacritic](https://www.metacritic.com/)** — film/TV/games/music. 0–100 Metascore. Weighted critic average. *Weakness:* undisclosed weights; user-score review bombing.
- **[OpenCritic](https://opencritic.com/)** — games. Top Critic Average (transparent, unweighted mean). *Weakness:* no user component; small samples for niche titles.
- **[Steam user reviews](https://store.steampowered.com/)** — games. Positive/negative tiers, "Recent" vs "All-time". Owner-gated binary. *Weakness:* protest review bombing.
- **[Goodreads](https://www.goodreads.com/)** — books. 1–5 simple average. Crowd, minimal verification. *Weakness:* sockpuppet scandals; pre-publication bombing of unreleased books.
- **[Letterboxd](https://letterboxd.com/)** — film. 0.5–5 stars, weighted average. Cinephile crowd.
- **[RateYourMusic](https://rateyourmusic.com/)** — music. Credibility-weighted crowd charts. *Weakness:* opaque user-weighting; canon/obscurity skew.
- **[MyAnimeList](https://myanimelist.net/)** / **[AniList](https://anilist.co/)** — anime/manga. Bayesian-weighted scores. *Weakness:* score inflation; seasonal brigading.
- **[Billboard charts](https://www.billboard.com/charts/)** — songs/albums. Weekly ranking. Statistical blend of streams + sales + airplay. *Weakness:* bundling/stream-campaign manipulation; opaque weights.
- **[Pitchfork](https://pitchfork.com/)** — albums. Single critic 0.0–10.0. *Weakness:* single-reviewer subjectivity.
- **[Nielsen](https://www.nielsen.com/)** — TV/streaming audience. Ratings/share. Panel + (since 2025) big-data hybrid. *Weakness:* panel sampling error for niche audiences; clients are the rated networks.
- **[Common Sense Media](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/)** — media for kids. Age (2–18) + 5-star quality. Expert reviewers on child-development criteria; nonprofit.
- **Age/content boards** — **[MPA](https://www.motionpictures.org/film-ratings/)** (G–NC-17, anonymous parent panel), **[ESRB](https://www.esrb.org/)** (games), **[PEGI](https://pegi.info/)** (games). Self-regulatory; rely on publisher disclosure (hidden content can slip).

## Finance, credit, insurance & risk

- **[FICO](https://www.fico.com/)** / **[VantageScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VantageScore)** — consumer credit. 300–850. Proprietary statistical model. *Weakness:* opacity; thin-file exclusion; entrenched gatekeeper.
- **Credit bureaus** — **[Experian](https://www.experian.com/)**, **[Equifax](https://www.equifax.com/)**, **[TransUnion](https://www.transunion.com/)**. Full credit reports. Data aggregation. *Weakness:* common data errors hard to dispute; the 2017 Equifax breach (~147M people).
- **Bond/sovereign ratings** — **[Moody's](https://www.moodys.com/)**, **[S&P Global](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/)**, **[Fitch](https://www.fitchratings.com/)**. AAA–D letter scales. Analyst committee + models, **issuer-pays**. *Weakness:* the canonical capture story — inflated AAA on mortgage securities; S&P settled with the US Justice Department and states for \$1.375B (2015) and Moody's for about \$864M (2017).
- **[Morningstar](https://www.morningstar.com/)** — funds/stocks. 1–5 stars (quant, backward-looking), Medalist (forward-looking), Economic Moat. *Weakness:* star ratings weakly predict future performance; "star chasing".
- **ESG ratings** — **[MSCI](https://www.msci.com/our-solutions/esg-investing/esg-ratings)** (AAA–CCC), **[Sustainalytics](https://www.sustainalytics.com/)** (0–100 risk), **[S&P Global ESG](https://www.spglobal.com/esg/)**. *Weakness:* ratings divergence — correlations between six ESG raters average 0.54 (range 0.38–0.71), against 0.99 for credit ratings ([Berg, Kölbel & Rigobon, *Review of Finance* 2022](https://academic.oup.com/rof/article/26/6/1315/6590670)).
- **[A.M. Best](https://www.ambest.com/)** — insurer financial strength. A++–F. Insurance-specialist analysis; largely issuer-pays.
- **Credit-based insurance scores** — **[LexisNexis](https://risk.lexisnexis.com/products/attract)**, FICO. Risk scores for underwriting. *Weakness:* fairness/proxy-discrimination concerns; restricted or banned in several US states.
- **[Zillow Zestimate](https://www.zillow.com/zestimate/)** — home value. Dollar estimate + range. ML automated valuation. *Weakness:* off-market median error ~7%; ignores condition; "not an appraisal".
- **Cyber risk** — **[BitSight](https://www.bitsight.com/security-ratings)** (250–900), **[SecurityScorecard](https://securityscorecard.com/)** (A–F), **[CVSS](https://www.first.org/cvss/)** (0–10, open standard). *Weakness:* external-only signals; CVSS severity routinely conflated with risk → "everything is Critical".
- **[Dun & Bradstreet PAYDEX](https://www.dnb.com/)** — business payment reliability. 1–100. Vendor-reported trade data.

## Academia, science & education

- **Scholarly peer review** — manuscripts. Accept/revise/reject. Expert review, mostly unpaid. *Weakness:* low inter-rater reliability ("lottery"); slow; weak fraud screening.
- **[Journal Impact Factor](https://jcr.clarivate.com/)** (Clarivate) — journals. Citation ratio. *Weakness:* heavily gamed (coercive/self-citation, cartels); [DORA](https://sfdora.org/) condemns its use to judge individuals.
- **h-index** — authors. Single integer (productivity × impact). *Weakness:* field-dependent; gameable via self-citation; can't decrease.
- **Citation databases** — **[Web of Science](https://clarivate.com/)**, **[Scopus](https://www.scopus.com/)** (Elsevier — also a publisher), **[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/)** (widest, least curated).
- **[Altmetric](https://www.altmetric.com/)** — online attention. Weighted "donut" score. *Weakness:* measures attention, not quality; gameable.
- **University rankings** — **[QS](https://www.topuniversities.com/world-university-rankings)**, **[THE](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings)** (reputation-survey heavy), **[ARWU/Shanghai](https://www.shanghairanking.com/)** (objective, prize-weighted), **[US News](https://www.usnews.com/best-colleges)** (self-reported data enabled the Columbia fraud; 2023 boycott), **[Leiden](https://www.leidenranking.com/)** (bibliometric, deliberately no composite).
- **[REF](https://2029.ref.ac.uk/)** (UK Research Excellence Framework) — university research. 4*–1* profiles. Expert panel review; allocates ~£2B/yr. *Weakness:* very high administrative cost.
- **[GRADE](https://www.gradeworkinggroup.org/)** / **[Cochrane RoB 2](https://methods.cochrane.org/risk-bias-2)** — evidence quality / trial bias. Tiered ratings. Structured expert rating. *Weakness:* domain judgments still subjective.
- **Standardized tests** — **[SAT/ACT](https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat)**, **[GRE](https://www.ets.org/gre.html)**, **[PISA](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/programmes/pisa.html)**, **[TIMSS](https://www.iea.nl/studies/iea/timss)**. *Weakness:* scores track family income; teaching-to-the-test.
- **School ratings** — **[GreatSchools](https://www.greatschools.org/)** (1–10; historically correlated with race/affluence), **[Ofsted](https://reports.ofsted.gov.uk/)** (England; replaced single-word grades with report cards in 2025 after criticism).
- **Accreditation** — **[ABET](https://www.abet.org/)** (engineering/computing), **[AACSB](https://www.aacsb.edu/)** (business schools), US institutional accreditors (Title IV gatekeepers). *Weakness:* peers accredit peers (conflict); slow on failing schools.

## Health, safety, standards & certification

- **Hospital ratings** — **[CMS star ratings](https://www.medicare.gov/care-compare/)** (1–5, federal), **[Leapfrog](https://www.hospitalsafetygrade.org/)** (A–F safety), **[US News Best Hospitals](https://health.usnews.com/best-hospitals)**, **[Healthgrades](https://www.healthgrades.com/)**. *Weakness:* CMS criticized for penalizing complex/teaching hospitals; Healthgrades and Leapfrog charge hospitals to license their grades for marketing. In March 2026 a federal judge ruled that Leapfrog's revised method, which gave hospitals that skipped its voluntary survey the lowest possible score on some measures it lacked data for, violated Florida consumer-protection law, and ordered five such hospitals' grades removed; Leapfrog is appealing ([WUSF](https://www.wusf.org/health-news-florida/2026-09-10/leapfrog-appeals-judges-ruling-for-south-florida-hospitals-over-safety-grades)).
- **Restaurant hygiene** — **[NYC letter grades](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/business/food-operators/letter-grading-for-restaurants.page)** (A/B/C), **[UK Food Hygiene Rating Scheme](https://www.food.gov.uk/safety-hygiene/food-hygiene-rating-scheme)** (0–5). Unannounced inspections; municipal, no fee-for-grade. *Weakness:* snapshot validity; inspection inconsistency.
- **Drug/device** — **[FDA](https://www.fda.gov/)**, **[EMA](https://www.ema.europa.eu/)**, **[NICE](https://www.nice.org.uk/)** (cost-per-QALY HTA). Approve/not. Expert regulatory review. *Weakness:* user-fee funding criticized as "cozy"; QALY thresholds called arbitrary.
- **Crash tests** — **[IIHS](https://www.iihs.org/)** (Good–Poor + Top Safety Pick; insurer-funded, independent of makers), **[Euro NCAP](https://www.euroncap.com/)** (0–5 stars), **[NHTSA 5-Star](https://www.nhtsa.gov/ratings)** (most cluster at 4–5★). *Weakness:* limited scenario set; "test to the test".
- **Product safety** — **[UL](https://www.ul.com/)** (lab testing + factory audits, fee-for-cert), **[CE marking](https://europa.eu/youreurope/business/product-requirements/labels-markings/ce-marking/index_en.htm)** (mostly self-declared). *Weakness:* UL cost barrier + counterfeit marks; CE self-declaration is gameable.
- **Energy** — **[Energy Star](https://www.energystar.gov/)** (a 2010 GAO sting certified a gas-powered "alarm clock" → triggered third-party testing), **[EU energy label](https://energy-efficient-products.ec.europa.eu/)** (A–G; rescaled 2021).
- **[ISO 9001 certification](https://www.iso.org/iso-9001-quality-management.html)** — quality-management systems. Pass/fail + surveillance audits. Third-party audit, **client pays the auditor**. *Weakness:* "audit shopping"; certifies process not outcome.
- **[LEED](https://www.usgbc.org/leed)** — green buildings. Certified–Platinum, points-based; fee-for-cert. *Weakness:* design- not performance-based — certified buildings don't reliably use less energy.
- **[B Corp](https://www.bcorporation.net/)** — whole-company social/environmental. Pass/fail seal (≥80/200); fee-for-cert. *Weakness:* bar seen as low; Dr. Bronner's dropped the cert in 2025 over multinational dilution.
- **Food/agriculture** — **[USDA Organic](https://www.ams.usda.gov/about-ams/programs-offices/national-organic-program)**, **[Fairtrade](https://www.fairtrade.net/)**, **[MSC](https://www.msc.org/)** seafood (logo-royalty conflict), **[Rainforest Alliance](https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/)**. *Weakness:* royalty/fee models create incentives to certify generously.

## Hospitality, travel & local business

- **[Michelin Guide](https://guide.michelin.com/)** — restaurants/hotels. 1–3 stars. Professional anonymous inspectors, multiple visits. *Weakness:* tourism boards increasingly pay for regional entry (conflict); fine-dining/Eurocentric bias.
- **[AAA Diamonds](https://www.aaa.com/diamonds/)** — N. American hotels/restaurants. 1–5 Diamonds. Anonymous inspectors; nonprofit. **[Forbes Travel Guide](https://www.forbestravelguide.com/)** — luxury. 4–5 Star. Inspectors on ~900 standards. *Weakness:* Forbes also sells training on how to earn its ratings.
- **Hotel star systems** — accommodations. 1–5 stars. **[Hotelstars Union](https://www.hotelstars.eu/)** standardizes 21 European countries; the US has no government system (self-declared "5-star" is meaningless).
- **[Yelp](https://www.yelp.com/)** — local businesses. 1–5 stars + automated review filter. *Weakness:* long-running extortion / pay-to-play allegations.
- **[TripAdvisor](https://www.tripadvisor.com/)** — travel. 1–5 bubbles. Crowd, no proof of stay. *Weakness:* a 2018 investigation alleged ~1 in 3 reviews fake; 200k+ AI-generated reviews removed in 2024.
- **[Google Reviews](https://maps.google.com/)** — places. 1–5 stars + AI moderation. *Weakness:* ~240M fake reviews removed in 2024; extortion scams at scale.
- **[Booking.com](https://www.booking.com/reviews_guidelines.html)** / **Hotels.com** — accommodations. Score /10, **verified guests only**, recency-weighted. *Weakness:* commission model is a structural conflict.
- **[Trustpilot](https://www.trustpilot.com/)** — businesses. TrustScore (Bayesian-weighted). *Weakness:* paying businesses get more tools (two-tier criticism).
- **[BBB grades](https://www.bbb.org/)** — business trustworthiness. A+–F. Composite + accreditation fees. *Weakness:* in 2010 Los Angeles business owners got a fictitious business named "Hamas" accredited with an A− by paying \$425, as ABC's *20/20* [reported](https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/better-business-bureau-accused-of-pay-to-play-scheme/) (pay-for-grade); the Los Angeles chapter was expelled in 2013.
- **[Glassdoor](https://www.glassdoor.com/)** — employers. 1–5 stars, anonymous, "give to get". *Weakness:* anonymity enables fakes; the rated employer pays the host.

## Online platforms & reputation systems

- **[eBay feedback](https://www.ebay.com/help/buying/resolving-issues-sellers/seller-ratings?id=4023)** — sellers. % positive + detailed star ratings. Transaction-linked. *Weakness:* extreme grade inflation; seller retaliation led eBay to bar negative buyer feedback.
- **[Amazon reviews](https://www.amazon.com/)** — products/sellers. 1–5 stars + Verified Purchase. ML-weighted crowd. *Weakness:* persistent fake/incentivized reviews; the FTC's 2024 fake-review rule targets this.
- **[Airbnb](https://www.airbnb.com/)** — hosts/guests. 1–5 stars, **double-blind reveal**, Superhost badge. *Weakness:* retaliation/extortion via review leverage; strong inflation (~4.8+ norm).
- **[Uber](https://www.uber.com/)** / **[Lyft](https://www.lyft.com/)** — drivers/riders. 1–5 reciprocal rolling average. *Weakness:* drivers deactivated below ~4.6; a 2020 suit alleged aggregating biased customer ratings is discriminatory.
- **[DoorDash](https://help.doordash.com/)** — Dashers. 1–5 (last 100) + completion %. *Weakness:* low deactivation thresholds; ratings reflect restaurant/app delays outside the driver's control.
- **[Stack Overflow reputation](https://stackoverflow.com/help/whats-reputation)** — Q&A expertise. Points + privilege tiers. *Weakness:* voting rings / sockpuppets ([study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.07101)).
- **[GitHub stars](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/exploring-projects-on-github/saving-repositories-with-stars)** — repo popularity. Integer count. *Weakness:* a fake-star economy — millions of bought stars, often promoting malware ([study](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.13459v2)).
- **[Reddit karma](https://support.reddithelp.com/hc/en-us/articles/204511829-What-is-karma)** — contribution. Numeric. *Weakness:* karma farming via reposts/bots.
- **App store ratings** — **[Apple](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/ratings-and-reviews/)** (legacy ratings persist), **[Google Play](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/138230)** (recency-weighted). *Weakness:* bought reviews + review bombing.
- **[Wikipedia pending-changes / editor trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reviewing_pending_changes)** — editor trustworthiness. Permission flags + edit counts. Automated thresholds + admin grants. *Weakness:* edit count is a shallow, gameable proxy.

## Sports & competition rankings

- **[Elo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elo_rating_system)** / **[Glicko-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glicko_rating_system)** — player skill. Numeric rating (Glicko adds a confidence/deviation term). Zero-sum statistical update. *Weakness:* single K-factor models uncertainty crudely; pool-wide inflation.
- **[FIDE](https://www.fide.com/)** — chess. Elo with tiered K-factors. *Weakness:* decades-long inflation debates.
- **[ATP](https://www.atptour.com/en/rankings/rankings-faq)** / **[WTA](https://www.wtatennis.com/rankings-explained)** — tennis. Rolling 52-week points. *Weakness:* no opponent-strength weighting.
- **[OWGR](https://www.owgr.com/)** — golf. Strength-of-field-weighted points. *Weakness:* the LIV Golf exclusion controversy.
- **[FIFA rankings](https://inside.fifa.com/fifa-world-ranking/procedure-men)** — national football teams. Elo-based "SUM" model (since 2018, fixing the gameable old system).
- **Sabermetrics / WAR** — baseball player value, in wins. Statistical composite. *Weakness:* the two main versions ([bWAR](https://www.baseball-reference.com/about/war_explained.shtml), [fWAR](https://library.fangraphs.com/misc/war/)) disagree — "which WAR?".
- **[College Football Playoff](https://collegefootballplayoff.com/)** committee, **[AP Poll](https://apnews.com/hub/ap-top-25-college-football-poll)**, **Coaches Poll** — top-25 rankings. Expert/voter judgment. *Weakness:* opacity, reputation bias, and (Coaches Poll) direct conflicts of interest.

## Governance & social indices

- **[Corruption Perceptions Index](https://www.transparency.org/en/cpi/)** (Transparency International) — public-sector corruption. 0–100. Composite of expert/business surveys. *Weakness:* measures perceptions, not corruption.
- **[Freedom in the World](https://freedomhouse.org/report/freedom-world)** (Freedom House) — political rights/civil liberties. 0–100 + Free/Partly/Not Free. Expert assessment. *Weakness:* majority US-government funded (independence critique).
- **[V-Dem](https://www.v-dem.net/)** — democracy (5 dimensions). 0–1 indices. ~3,500 expert coders → Bayesian IRT with explicit uncertainty bounds. *Weakness:* expert-coding subjectivity; complex to audit.
- **[EIU Democracy Index](https://www.eiu.com/)** — democracy. 0–10 + regime type. *Weakness:* opaque, proprietary, anonymous experts.
- **[Human Development Index](https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/human-development-index)** (UNDP) — health/education/income. 0–1. Geometric mean of three indicators. *Weakness:* only three crude dimensions; arbitrary weighting.
- **[World Press Freedom Index](https://rsf.org/en/index)** (RSF) — press freedom. 0–100. Abuse tally + expert survey.
- **[Worldwide Governance Indicators](https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/worldwide-governance-indicators)** (World Bank) — six governance dimensions, with standard errors.
- **World Bank *Doing Business* (DISCONTINUED)** — ease of doing business. Killed in [September 2021](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/statement/2021/09/16/world-bank-group-to-discontinue-doing-business-report) after audits found **deliberate data manipulation** favoring certain countries under leadership pressure — the cleanest documented case of index capture.
- **[Gallup World Poll / World Happiness Report](https://worldhappiness.report/)** — wellbeing. Survey means (Cantril Ladder 0–10). Large-N self-report (not expert perception). *Weakness:* translation/cultural bias; over-reading a single question.
- *Also:* [Global Peace Index](https://www.economicsandpeace.org/global-peace-index/), [WJP Rule of Law Index](https://worldjusticeproject.org/rule-of-law-index/), [Environmental Performance Index](https://epi.yale.edu/), and the ideologically-framed economic-freedom indices ([Heritage](https://www.heritage.org/index/), [Fraser](https://www.fraserinstitute.org/economic-freedom)).

## Charity & nonprofit evaluation

- **[GiveWell](https://www.givewell.org/)** — global health/development charities. Short "Top Charities" list + cost-per-life-saved estimates. Deep in-house CEA, publishes full models. *Weakness:* very narrow, evidence-rich cause focus.
- **[Charity Navigator](https://www.charitynavigator.org/)** — US 501(c)(3)s. 0–4 stars / 0–100. Largely automated from Form 990s + impact "beacons". *Weakness:* historic overhead-ratio reliance is a poor, gameable impact proxy.
- **[Candid / GuideStar](https://www.guidestar.org/)** — nonprofit profiles. Bronze–Platinum transparency seals. Self-reported data. *Weakness:* seals measure disclosure, not effectiveness.
- **[Animal Charity Evaluators](https://animalcharityevaluators.org/)**, **[Founders Pledge](https://www.founderspledge.com/)** — impact-focused evaluation in harder-to-measure causes. **ImpactMatters** (cost-per-impact) was folded into Charity Navigator (2020).
- *Also:* [CharityWatch](https://www.charitywatch.org/) (A+–F), [BBB Wise Giving / Give.org](https://give.org/) (pass/fail accreditation), [Giving What We Can](https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/) (meta-evaluation of evaluators).

## Forecasting & prediction platforms

- **[Metaculus](https://www.metaculus.com/)** — many event types. Community-prediction probability; forecasters scored by proper rules. Crowd aggregation, no betting. *Weakness:* aggregate accuracy largely self-reported; money enters only through prize tournaments (e.g. the [AI forecasting benchmark series](https://www.metaculus.com/aib/)).
- **[Good Judgment](https://goodjudgment.com/)** / **[GJ Open](https://www.gjopen.com/)** — geopolitics/economics. Probabilities scored by Brier; curated Superforecasters. *Weakness:* premium forecasts paywalled; small expert panel.
- **[Polymarket](https://polymarket.com/)** — real-world events. Market price = probability; real-money crypto. *Weakness:* left the US after a 2022 CFTC settlement and returned via its 2025 purchase of the CFTC-licensed exchange QCEX; thin-market manipulation.
- **[Kalshi](https://kalshi.com/)** — US event contracts. Binary \$0–\$1; CFTC-regulated exchange. *Weakness:* much volume is sports, not forecasting.
- **[Manifold](https://manifold.markets/)** — user-created markets. Play-money market maker. *Weakness:* play money weakens incentives; creator-resolved miscalibration.
- **[PredictIt](https://www.predictit.org/)** — US politics. Real-money, academic project. *Weakness:* position/withdrawal caps distort prices.

## AI models & public information

- **[Arena](https://arena.ai/)** (Chatbot Arena, then LMArena; [renamed](https://arena.ai/blog/lmarena-is-now-arena/) January 2026) — LLMs. Bradley–Terry/Elo leaderboard from crowd pairwise votes. Venture-funded; since September 2025 it also [sells evaluations](https://arena.ai/blog/ai-evaluations/) to model labs and enterprises. *Weakness:* labs can test private variants and publish the best ([Singh et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879) count 27 private variants from Meta before Llama 4). In April 2025 Meta's leaderboard entry was a non-public, chat-tuned variant; the operator apologised and changed its policy ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2025/04/11/metas-vanilla-maverick-ai-model-ranks-below-rivals-on-a-popular-chat-benchmark)).
- **X Community Notes** (formerly Birdwatch) — context notes on posts. A matrix-factorisation "bridging" algorithm favours notes rated helpful across groups of raters who usually disagree, so one faction cannot carry a note alone ([Wojcik et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.15723)). Meta replaced US third-party fact-checking with the same model in 2025 ([Meta](https://about.fb.com/news/2025/01/meta-more-speech-fewer-mistakes/)). Since mid-2025 LLM "AI writers" may propose notes, which human raters still score; in a three-month field test one team's LLM notes were rated more helpful than human notes on the same posts ([Li & Bakker 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02592)).
- **[The Unjournal](https://unjournal.org/)** — economics, policy and social-science research. Commissions paid, public expert evaluations with ratings. Grant-funded nonprofit; charges authors nothing.
