- *Also (added after the coding):* Epoch AI's FrontierMath benchmark was funded by OpenAI, which owns its 300 core problems and has their solutions apart from a 50-problem holdout. The funding was disclosed only around the December 2024 announcement of o3's score on it, and Epoch [conceded](https://epoch.ai/blog/openai-and-frontiermath) it had not communicated the relationship clearly. With Arena's sales to model labs, it brings the rated-party-pays pattern into AI evaluation.

## Does who pays predict failure?

This page and [Patterns §3](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#3-incentives-and-funding-shape-trustworthiness) used to say that funding structure predicts trustworthiness better than method does. In October 2026 the catalogue was coded to test that. The data and script are in the repository ([`data/systems.csv`, `data/analyze.py`](https://github.com/quantified-uncertainty/cairn/tree/main/apps/evaluation-engineering/data)).

**Coding.** Each named system is one row (161; "Also" mentions excluded). Each row records:
- the primary payer: the evaluated party, users, a third party (advertisers, affiliate retailers, insurers, donors), the public, or mixed;
- whether the evaluated party pays the evaluator anything material, such as fees, commissions, advertising, or logo or award licences;
- the method family;
- any documented major failure. A failure counts as *established* when a regulator, court, official audit, peer-reviewed study, the operator itself or a named investigation found the outputs materially distorted. It counts as *alleged* when the system has only been criticised. Fakes that a platform merely removed do not count, and neither do single disputed ratings.

The result was 42 established failures, each sourced in the CSV, 19 alleged, and 100 with none found.

**Results.** 154 systems have a known payer, and 41 of them have an established failure.
- *The payer typology predicts nothing detectable.* Failure rates run from 19% (user-paid) to 34% (paid by the evaluated party), well within noise (permutation test p = 0.72). In leave-one-out prediction, knowing the payer category does slightly worse than ignoring it.
- *Method does little better.* Among the larger method families, testing and inspection have the lowest failure rate (12%) and crowd systems the highest (39%), but p = 0.23 and the predictive gain is nil. Across bootstrap resamples of catalogue entries, payer came out ahead of method in 27%: no clear winner either way.
- *One contrast does hold up: does the rated party pay at all?* Where it does, 27 of 67 systems (40%) have an established failure; where it does not, 10 of 62 (16%). That is an odds ratio of 3.5 (90% CI 1.6–7.8, Fisher p = 0.003). The odds ratio stays between 2.6 and 4.9 within method families, after dropping low-confidence codings, with each catalogue bullet counted once, and whichever way the 25 unknowns are assigned.
- *Those failures are more often gaming than capture.* Of the 27, 6 are capture in the strict sense, meaning a lenient rating of the payer: the three agencies' 2008 credit ratings, the BBB, the ACICS accreditor and the FDA's Aduhelm approval. Eleven are manipulation by the rated party or outsiders (fake reviews, falsified rankings data, leaked tests); the other ten concern validity or data quality. Capture and evaluator misconduct together are rare (7 of 154), too rare to test on their own.

**Caveats.** Treat this as weak evidence.
- *Selection.* A failure is counted only if someone documented it. Firms paid by the parties they rate attract regulators, litigants and journalists, so "none found" means "not found in a targeted search".
- *Coder bias.* One coder, not blind: payer and failure were coded from the same reading.
- *Multiple tests.* Three codings were tested and none was pre-registered; correcting for three tests puts the binary contrast at p ≈ 0.01.
- *A broad variable.* "Pays anything" lumps issuer fees with advertising, marketplace commissions and products sold to the rated party (the three credit bureaus qualify because consumers buy monitoring from them). The contrast is not concentrated where certification theory puts it: where the rated party is the main payer, 12 of 35 systems have an established failure (34%); where it pays only on the side, 15 of 32 (47%; Fisher p = 0.33). This split was examined after the main results.
- *Stakes as a confounder.* A rated party pays for a rating when the rating is worth a lot to it, and high stakes are what drive gaming ([Patterns §1](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#1-the-measure-reshapes-the-measured)). Because gaming outnumbers leniency almost two to one in the paying group, the data fit "payment marks high-stakes ratings" at least as well as "payment buys the evaluator".

The claim as stated is not supported. What survives is narrower: when the rated party pays the evaluator, the odds of a documented failure are about 3.5 times higher, and the mechanism is unresolved.

## Lessons for evaluation engineering

The literature behind each lesson is on [Patterns & Failure Modes](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/).

1. **Whether the rated party pays matters; the finer funding story did not survive coding.** See [above](#does-who-pays-predict-failure): higher odds of documented failure, mostly through gaming; the leniency that [certification economics](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#3-incentives-and-funding-shape-trustworthiness) predicts accounts for only 6 of the 27 failures.
2. **Every output format is gameable, differently.** Binary fresh/rotten invites bombing; 100-point scales inflate and compress; reciprocal two-sided ratings breed retaliation and inflation; self-declared certifications get faked. Choosing the [output format](/concepts/the-systems-view/) is choosing your failure mode.
3. **Crowd systems converge on the same arms race** (fakes, astroturfing, review bombing) and the same defences: verified purchase or stay, credibility and recency weighting, and ML fraud detection.
4. **Composite indices live or die on weighting**, which is inherently contested (HDI's three dimensions, ESG divergence, ranking methodology churn). The [OECD composite-indicators handbook](/reference/adjacent-fields/) exists precisely because this is hard.
5. **Cheap, standardized ratings can change behaviour at scale.** Los Angeles's hygiene grade cards cut foodborne-illness hospitalizations ([Patterns §3](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/#3-incentives-and-funding-shape-trustworthiness)), though New York's inspections proved inconsistent and crash ratings invite testing to the test. That is the [systems view](/concepts/the-systems-view/#the-design-space)'s trade of accuracy for unit cost, made many times already.

## Meta-lists & further reading

Curated catalogues of evaluation systems (the "good lists" that already exist):

- **Wikipedia — [List of international rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_international_rankings)** — the best single index of country rankings by domain.
- **Wikipedia categories** — [Review websites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Review_websites), [International rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:International_rankings), [Credit rating agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Credit_rating_agencies), [Certification marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Certification_marks).
- **Wikipedia overviews** — [Review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator), [Reputation system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reputation_system), [List of academic databases and search engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_academic_databases_and_search_engines), [Sustainability standards and certification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainability_standards_and_certification), [List of freedom indices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_freedom_indices).
- **[Ecolabel Index](https://www.ecolabelindex.com/)** — a directory of ~450+ ecolabels across ~200 countries.
- **Academic** — Davis, Kingsbury & Merry, *[Governance by Indicators](https://academic.oup.com/book/32690)* (Oxford, 2012) — the scholarly catalogue + critique of global indicators; Jøsang et al., *[A survey of trust and reputation systems](https://people.cs.vt.edu/~irchen/5984/pdf/Josang-DSS07.pdf)* (2007); Tadelis, *[Reputation and Feedback Systems in Online Platform Markets](https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/stadelis/Annual_Review_Tadelis.pdf)* (2016).

See also [Adjacent Fields & Literature](/reference/adjacent-fields/) for the academic disciplines behind these systems, and [Related Work](/reference/related-work/) for QURI's own evaluation tools.


------------------------------------------------------------
## 14. Patterns & Failure Modes
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: early draft, synthesized from a June 2026 literature sweep. This is the analytical companion to [Evaluation Systems in the Wild](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/): the catalogue lists about 160 systems; this page asks what is **repeatedly found** across them. Each pattern names a mechanism, the key papers, and the real systems that illustrate it.*

Citations and key figures were checked against their sources (June 2026, with spot corrections in October 2026). Interpretive glosses, including the design implications, are this wiki's, not the cited authors'. A "~" denotes a rounded or pooled value (e.g. a meta-analytic mean); check the original for exact numbers and confidence intervals.

The findings cluster into five families. The first is the most consequential for this field: **a public evaluation changes what it measures.**

## 1. The measure reshapes the measured

Deploying a public evaluation is an *intervention* as well as an observation. Espeland & Sauder call this **reactivity** — "how public measures recreate social worlds" ([*AJS* 2007](https://doi.org/10.1086/517897); book-length in [*Engines of Anxiety*](https://www.russellsage.org/publications/engines-anxiety), 2016) — and identify two mechanisms:

- **Self-fulfilling prophecy.** Once a measure is authoritative, audiences act on it, making it true. A law school that drops a US News tier gets weaker applicants, less alumni giving, and worse placement — becoming actually worse, confirming the rank.
- **Commensuration** ([Espeland & Stevens, *Ann. Rev. Sociology* 1998](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.soc.24.1.313)). Collapsing diverse qualities into one number erases information *and* reorganizes how the rated parties think and allocate effort. Power flows to whoever defines the metric — its categories, inputs, and weights.

Reactivity's destructive twin is **Goodhart's law**. [Goodhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law) (1975, monetary policy) and [Campbell](https://doi.org/10.1016/0149-7189(79)90048-X) (1979, from a 1976 paper; social indicators) stated it independently, and the [Lucas critique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_critique) (1976) made the related point that policy changes break the econometric relationships they rely on. Campbell adds a *dose–response* claim: corruption scales with the stakes attached. The popular phrasing, "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure," is Strathern's gloss ([1997](https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1234-981X(199707)5:3%3C305::AID-EURO184%3E3.0.CO;2-4)), often misattributed to Goodhart.

[Manheim & Garrabrant (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.04585) give the precise decomposition. When proxy *M* is optimized for hidden goal *G*, four distinct things go wrong, and **three require no bad actor**:

| Variant | Mechanism | Adversary needed? |
|---|---|---|
| **Regressional** | *M = G + noise*; the top of *M* selects partly for noise (winner's curse) | No |
| **Extremal** | the *M*–*G* correlation breaks down in the extreme region optimization reaches | No |
| **Causal** | *M* correlates with *G* but isn't causally upstream — intervening doesn't move *G* | No |
| **Adversarial** | an agent who knows you optimize *M* manipulates it (incl. the "cobra effect" where the metric's own incentive backfires) | Yes |

Two further mechanisms matter. **Surrogation** ([Choi, Hecht & Tayler 2012](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1438212)): people don't just game the proxy cynically — they *psychologically substitute* it for the goal, strongest when a single measure is tied to pay. And a behavioral severity ladder ([Bevan & Hood 2006](https://eprints.lse.ac.uk/16211/), on NHS targets): **effort substitution** ("hitting the target and missing the point") → **gaming** (meeting the letter, subverting the purpose) → **outright fabrication**. Effort substitution has a formal model: when an agent does several tasks and only some are measured, strong incentives on the measured ones pull effort from the rest, so the best contract may offer weak incentives or a flat wage ([Holmström & Milgrom 1991](https://doi.org/10.1093/jleo/7.special_issue.24)).

The same law governs optimization against automated evaluators, from learned reward models ([Gao, Schulman & Hilton 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760)) to monitors: when a chain-of-thought monitor's verdict was added to a reasoning model's training reward, strong optimization taught the model to hide its intent while still reward hacking ([Baker et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926)). [LLM Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#the-two-system-level-failures) takes up what this means for model judges.

**Seen in the wild:** US News rankings (reactivity — schools restructure around the formula; [a 2022–23 revolt](https://www.usnews.com/best-colleges) saw many top law/medical schools withdraw); Journal Impact Factor (adversarial — coercive self-citation, [Wilhite & Fong, *Science* 2012](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1212540); citation cartels); credit ratings (adversarial — issuer "ratings shopping"); NHS waiting-time gaming; cardiac-surgery report cards (adversarial, by selecting on inputs — surgeons avoid sick patients, below).

> **Design implication.** Gaming rises with the stakes on a measure (Campbell) and with its predictability. The levers are to lower the stakes on any single measure, to measure the neglected tasks or weaken incentives on the measured ones, to keep the metric definition out of the rated parties' hands, and to add randomness to assessment (random audits, rotating or held-out items), at some cost to transparency ([Bevan & Hood 2004](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.328.7440.598)). The sibling [RRP](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/hardening-invariance/) wiki's hardening chapters develop the versions for automated evaluators.

## 2. The ratings you collect are a biased sample

Even setting aside gaming, the raw ratings entering a system are not a clean sample of quality.

- **Distributions are J-shaped / bimodal, from self-selection.** Online ratings pile up at 5 stars with a 1-star spike and little middle ([Hu, Pavlou & Zhang, *CACM* 2009](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1562764.1562800); [*MISQ* 2017](https://misq.umn.edu/misq/article/41/2/449/335/On-Self-Selection-Biases-in-Online-Product)). Two mechanisms: **acquisition bias** (buyers already liked the product) and **under-reporting / "brag-and-moan" bias** (only extreme experiences bother to review). The mean is therefore a biased signal; the full distribution predicts behavior better.
- **Social influence herds, asymmetrically.** In a randomized experiment on >100,000 comments, a single seeded *positive* vote made the next viewer ~32% more likely to up-vote and, through accumulating herding, raised the comment's final mean rating by ~25%; a seeded *negative* vote was *corrected* by the crowd ([Muchnik, Aral & Taylor, *Science* 2013](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1240466)). Positive herding accumulates; negative does not.
- **Expert review has low inter-rater reliability.** A meta-analysis of peer review (48 studies, ~19,443 manuscripts) found mean agreement ICC ≈ 0.34, κ ≈ 0.17 ([Bornmann, Mutz & Daniel, *PLoS ONE* 2010](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0014331)); the classic NSF re-review found funding "depends to a significant extent on chance" — i.e., on *which* reviewers are drawn ([Cole, Cole & Simon, *Science* 1981](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.7302566)).
- **Scales drift and compress.** Grade inflation is the canonical case: the A-share rose from ~15% of grades (1940) to over 40% (2008), making A the most common grade ([Rojstaczer & Healy 2012](https://www.gradeinflation.com/tcr2012grading.pdf)). The ceiling compresses and the signal degrades — the same shape as reputation inflation (§4).
- **Fakes are detectable but persistent.** Crowdsourced fake reviews have linguistic signatures a classifier catches at ~90% where humans are near chance ([Ott et al., *ACL* 2011](https://aclanthology.org/P11-1032/)), but on reviews Yelp's filter had flagged, linguistic features did much worse than behavioural ones such as posting patterns ([Mukherjee et al., *ICWSM* 2013](https://doi.org/10.1609/icwsm.v7i1.14389)). Requiring a verified purchase raises the cost of faking and measurably reduces — but doesn't eliminate — manipulation ([Mayzlin, Dover & Chevalier, *AER* 2014](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.104.8.2421)).

**Seen in the wild:** Amazon's J-shape (and its Verified-Purchase badge as the Mayzlin fix); IMDb's 1/10 polarization (and its Bayesian weighting as the §5 fix); Reddit/HN early-vote snowball (and vote-fuzzing / "controversial" sort as countermeasures); peer review and grant panels (low reliability → motivates more reviewers + calibration).

> **Design implication.** Don't treat the mean of self-selected ratings as the quality signal. Verify *who* is evaluating, model the selection process, and prefer distribution-aware metrics.

## 3. Incentives and funding shape trustworthiness

<a id="3-incentives-and-funding-decide-trustworthiness--more-than-method-does"></a>

The economics of quality disclosure predicts that who pays a certifier shapes what it certifies. A [coding of the catalogue](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/#does-who-pays-predict-failure) gives partial support: more documented failures where the rated party pays, but more of them gaming than lenient certification.

- **Quality information is valuable because of adverse selection.** When buyers can't tell quality, good sellers exit and markets collapse to "lemons" ([Akerlof, *QJE* 1970](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/84/3/488/1896241)). Evaluation systems exist to restore those lost gains from trade.
- **A signal works only if it's differentially costly** to fake for low-quality types ([Spence, *QJE* 1973](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/87/3/355/1909092)). The design question is always: *can a bad type cheaply mimic this?*
- **Voluntary disclosure should "unravel" to full disclosure — but often doesn't,** because receivers aren't fully skeptical, disclosure is costly, the sender may not know its own quality, and quality is multidimensional ([Grossman 1981](https://ideas.repec.org/a/ucp/jlawec/v24y1981i3p461-83.html); [Milgrom 1981](https://milgrom.people.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/1981/10/Good-News-and-Bad-News.pdf); survey: [Dranove & Jin, *JEL* 2010](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jel.48.4.935)). This is the case for *mandatory* disclosure.
- **When the rated party pays, the certifier prefers a coarse, lenient signal.** A profit-maximizing monopoly certifier optimally reveals only whether quality clears a low threshold ([Lizzeri, *RAND* 1999](https://ideas.repec.org/a/rje/randje/v30y1999isummerp214-231.html)); issuer-pays adds ratings shopping and inflation, worse in booms ([Bolton, Freixas & Shapiro, *J. Finance* 2012](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2011.01708.x)). Reputation disciplines certifiers only under strong conditions, and price *competition* can erode honesty rather than improve it ([Strausz 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167718704001092)). The evidence is contested: Fitch's growing market share coincided with higher, less informative incumbent ratings ([Becker & Milbourn, *JFE* 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2011.03.012)), but the association vanished once unobserved industry effects were controlled ([Bae, Kang & Wang, *JFQA* 2015](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109015000472)). Adding competitors is not a reliable fix.
- **Disclosure backfires when the rated party games the input mix instead of improving.** Risk-adjusted cardiac-surgery report cards led surgeons to avoid sick patients, worsening outcomes for the sickest, because providers know more about severity than any adjustment can capture ([Dranove, Kessler, McClellan & Satterthwaite, *JPE* 2003](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/374180)). It *works* when the metric resists gaming and demand responds: LA restaurant hygiene grade cards raised scores, shifted demand, and cut foodborne-illness hospitalizations partly via real improvement ([Jin & Leslie, *QJE* 2003](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/118/2/409/1899578)).
- **Too many labels destroy a label's value** — the "Groucho effect": small uncertainty about what a label *means* makes consumers infer the labeled product is marginal ([Harbaugh, Maxwell & Roussillon, *Mgmt Sci* 2011](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/mnsc.1110.1412)).
- **Gatekeepers fail in correlated, predictable ways** when they rent their reputation to the issuer who pays them ([Coffee, *Gatekeepers* 2006](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/gatekeepers-9780199288090)) — Enron, WorldCom, the 2008 ratings.

**Seen in the wild:** credit ratings (issuer-pays → inflation); LEED (fee-for-cert; certified New York City offices showed no collective energy savings: [Scofield, *Energy & Buildings* 2013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enbuild.2013.08.032)); hospital report cards (cream-skimming); restaurant hygiene (independent inspector + hard-to-game metric → LA grade cards worked, though NYC's inspections proved inconsistent: [Ho, *Yale LJ* 2012](https://www.yalelawjournal.org/pdf/1120_mparaxzn.pdf)).

> **Design implication.** Credible evaluation needs (a) a signal that is differentially costly to fake, (b) an independent payer or a strong reputational stake, (c) skeptical receivers, and (d) a clear standard. Mandatory, standardized disclosure has the better record than voluntary, issuer-paid coarse certification, provided the rated party cannot improve its score by choosing its inputs; risk adjustment alone did not prevent that.

## 4. Reputation systems converge on the same arms race

- **Reputation is real but modestly priced.** A matched-item eBay field experiment found established reputation raised willingness-to-pay ~8% ([Resnick et al., *Exp. Econ.* 2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10683-006-4309-2)).
- **Reputation inflation is the central pathology.** eBay feedback runs ~99% positive, so even high-90s scores barely discriminate between sellers; dividing positives by all transactions, so that silence counts against a seller, gives a measure that predicts whether buyers return ([Nosko & Tadelis, NBER 2015](https://www.nber.org/papers/w20830)). On a large online labour market the share of workers given a perfect rating rose from 33% to 85% in six years, while private ratings of the same jobs, never shown to the workers, fell ([Filippas, Horton & Golden, *Marketing Science* 2022](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.1350)). The authors attribute this to raters' reluctance to harm the person they rate; every market they studied was person-to-person.
- **Bilateral feedback causes retaliation,** so platforms moved to **blind / simultaneous-reveal or one-sided** feedback ([Bolton, Greiner & Ockenfels, *Mgmt Sci* 2013](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.1120.1609)). That fixes retaliation, not inflation: the labour market above already used simultaneous reveal.
- **But selection bias often dominates retaliation:** on Airbnb, *who chooses to review* biases scores more than retaliation, with "socially induced reciprocity" from face-to-face contact suppressing negatives ([Fradkin et al., *EC* 2015](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2764468.2764528)).
- **Cheap pseudonyms enable whitewashing** — abandon a bad identity, re-enter clean — so cooperation survives only via a costly "newcomers pay dues" convention ([Friedman & Resnick 2001](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1430-9134.2001.00173.x)); and without a trusted identity authority one party can mint many fake identities (the **Sybil attack**, [Douceur 2002](https://www.freehaven.net/anonbib/cache/sybil.pdf)) — the engine of fake reviews and ballot-stuffing.
- **Cold start is an efficiency loss, not just unfairness:** newcomers can't get the first transaction that would build reputation; subsidizing it and publishing detailed evaluations raised later earnings enough to indicate they had been inefficiently excluded ([Pallais, *AER* 2014](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.104.11.3565)). (Foundational survey: [Tadelis, *Ann. Rev. Econ.* 2016](https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/stadelis/Annual_Review_Tadelis.pdf).)

**Seen in the wild:** eBay (the most-studied — inflation, retaliation→one-sided ratings, EPP search ranking); Airbnb (double-blind reveal; selection bias; "New listing" badges); Uber (ceiling compression ~4.6+; face-to-face suppression; driver re-registration); Amazon/Yelp (Sybil fakes and the filters that fight them).

> **Design implication.** Verifying *who* evaluates, by tying identity to a scarce resource, is the recurring fix for fakes, and information-flow design (blind, one-sided, recency-weighted) is the fix for retaliation. Neither stops inflation; expect consequential scores to drift up, and recalibrate them against signals that cost the rater less to give, such as silence or private feedback. This is the [trust-network](/concepts/techniques/) problem in miniature.

## 5. The scale and the aggregation rule are not neutral

- **Naive averages mis-rank low-volume items.** A 100%-positive item with 2 votes outranks a 95%-positive item with 500 under mean sorting. Two principled fixes: the **Wilson score lower bound** for binary votes ([Evan Miller, 2009](https://www.evanmiller.org/how-not-to-sort-by-average-rating.html); Reddit's "best" sort) and **Bayesian shrinkage** toward a global prior weighted by volume ([IMDb's Top-250 formula](https://help.imdb.com/article/imdb/track-movies-tv/ratings-faq/G67Y87TFYYP6TWAV); [Trustpilot's TrustScore](https://support.trustpilot.com/hc/en-us/articles/201748946)). Both regularize the **cold-start** problem.
- **Scale granularity depends on who aggregates.** For one respondent, reliability, validity and discriminating power rose with the number of response categories up to about 7, test–retest reliability tended to fall beyond 10, and respondents preferred 10 points ([Preston & Colman, *Acta Psychologica* 2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10769936/)). For ranking items across many raters, an up/down vote removes differences in how raters use a scale and volume restores the resolution; 5-star scales behave nearly bimodally anyway (§2).
- **Pairwise comparison often beats absolute scores.** Humans judge "is A better than B?" more reliably than "rate A 1–5"; [Bradley–Terry (1952)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2334029) / Elo model this and sidestep scale-anchoring — now used to rank LLMs in preference arenas, where selective disclosure of privately tested variants has biased the rankings ([Singh et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879)). (Caveat: online Elo is order-sensitive; the static MLE is more robust; cyclic preferences break the model.)
- **The aggregation rule materially changes the ranking.** Mean vs. median vs. Bayesian vs. positional **Borda** vs. **Kemeny** (the maximum-likelihood, Condorcet-consistent — but NP-hard — rule) give genuinely different winners on the same votes ([Dwork et al., *WWW* 2001](http://static.cs.brown.edu/courses/csci2531/papers/rank2.pdf)). Arrow-style impossibility lurks underneath: there is no canonical "correct" aggregator.

> **Design implication.** Choosing the [output format and aggregation rule](/concepts/the-systems-view/) is choosing your failure mode and partly choosing your answer. Make it explicit and defensible; for sparse data, regularize (Wilson or Bayesian); when raters are noisy, prefer pairwise.

## What this means for evaluation engineering

Pulling the five families together:

1. **Deploying an evaluation changes what it measures.** Rated parties optimize the proxy, more so as the stakes rise, and a system that ignores this feedback loop will be gamed. Moderate stakes per measure, randomness in assessment and control of the metric definition are the levers (§1).
2. **Whether the rated party pays is the funding variable with some evidence behind it.** Theory predicts lenient certification when the rated party pays. The [catalogue coding](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/#does-who-pays-predict-failure) finds about 3.5 times the odds of documented failure in such systems, more often through gaming than leniency, and no signal in the broader payer typology. It cannot separate payment from stakes, so treat the payer as a design variable worth controlling, not a proven lever; [Evaluation as a System](/concepts/the-systems-view/#technical-and-institutional-design-variables) takes up the consequences.
3. **Raw ratings are a biased, gameable sample.** Verifying *who evaluates* and aggregating with the whole distribution in view are what separate signal from noise.
4. **Every output format and aggregation rule embeds a choice** with predictable, different failure modes. None is neutral.
5. **The hard problems are old and partly solved.** Adverse selection, signalling, unravelling, reputation inflation, shrinkage estimators and the reactivity of public measures have decades of theory and evidence behind them; an automated evaluation system should start from this literature, not rediscover it.

## Core references by theme

- **Reactivity & quantification:** Espeland & Sauder (AJS 2007); Espeland & Stevens (1998, 2008); Porter, *Trust in Numbers* (1995); Power, *The Audit Society* (1997); Merry, *The Seductions of Quantification* (2016); Muller, *The Tyranny of Metrics* (2018); Davis, Kingsbury & Merry, *Governance by Indicators* (2012).
- **Goodhart & gaming:** Goodhart (1975); Lucas (1976); Campbell (1979); Strathern (1997); Manheim & Garrabrant (2018); Holmström & Milgrom (1991); Bevan & Hood (2004, 2006); Choi, Hecht & Tayler (2012/2013); Krakovna (specification gaming); Gao, Schulman & Hilton (2022); Baker et al. (2025).
- **Rating bias:** Muchnik, Aral & Taylor (2013); Hu, Pavlou & Zhang (2009, 2017); Godes & Silva (2012); Bornmann et al. (2010); Cole et al. (1981); Ott et al. (2011); Mukherjee et al. (2013); Mayzlin et al. (2014); Rojstaczer & Healy (2012).
- **Certification & disclosure:** Akerlof (1970); Spence (1973); Grossman (1981); Milgrom (1981); Lizzeri (1999); Strausz (2005); Becker & Milbourn (2011); Bae, Kang & Wang (2015); Dranove & Jin (2010); Dranove et al. (2003); Jin & Leslie (2003); Bolton, Freixas & Shapiro (2012); Harbaugh et al. (2011); Coffee (2006).
- **Reputation systems:** Resnick et al. (2000); Dellarocas (2003); Resnick & Zeckhauser (2002); Resnick et al. (2006); Friedman & Resnick (2001); Douceur (2002); Bolton, Greiner & Ockenfels (2013); Nosko & Tadelis (2015); Filippas, Horton & Golden (2022); Fradkin et al. (2015); Pallais (2014); Tadelis (2016); Jøsang, Ismail & Boyd (2007).
- **Scales & aggregation:** Evan Miller (2009); Wilson (1927); Preston & Colman (2000); Bradley & Terry (1952); Elo (1978); Dwork et al. (2001); Hunter (2004).

See [Adjacent Fields & Literature](/reference/adjacent-fields/) for the broader disciplines and [Evaluation Systems in the Wild](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/) for the systems these patterns describe.

# Part IV — The Environment
================================================================================


------------------------------------------------------------
## 15. Epistemic Culture
Source: https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org/concepts/epistemic-culture/
------------------------------------------------------------

*Status: draft, rebuilt October 2026. The cases are documented; the lessons drawn from them are this wiki's reading, and the rollout advice is conjecture.*

## The claim

An evaluation system pointed at people or organizations changes the behaviour of the evaluated, and some of that change is aimed at the system itself: lawsuits, boycotts, lobbying, refusal to supply data, or quiet self-censorship by the evaluators. The 2021–22 notes called this the cultural constraint and guessed it might bind harder than any technical one ([crux 10](/start-here/key-questions/#on-the-environment)). The cases below do not settle that guess. They show what the pushback looks like and which designs attracted it.

## Cases

**Ofsted's single-word grades.** England's school inspectorate summarized each inspection in one headline word, from "outstanding" to "inadequate". In December 2023 a coroner recorded that the death of headteacher Ruth Perry was "suicide, contributed to by an Ofsted inspection carried out in November 2022", and warned that the system let a school with fixable safeguarding problems receive the same overall label as one inadequate in every area ([prevention of future deaths report](https://www.judiciary.uk/prevention-of-future-death-reports/ruth-perry-prevention-of-future-deaths-report/)). The government removed single headline grades for state schools in September 2024 ([DfE](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/single-headline-ofsted-grades-scrapped-in-landmark-school-reform)). Ofsted's replacement report cards grade each area separately on a five-point scale and give no overall judgement ([Ofsted guidance](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/understanding-ofsted-report-cards-and-grades)). The evaluation survived; its most compressed output did not.

**The US News law-school boycott.** In November 2022 Yale Law School, ranked first every year, withdrew from the US News rankings, calling them "profoundly flawed"; Harvard Law School followed the same day ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2022/11/16/yale-harvard-law-schools-dump-u-s-news-school-rankings/)). Rankings depend partly on data the ranked institutions supply, so the evaluated could exit. Their stated objection was that the formula rewarded behaviour they considered harmful, the reactivity Espeland and Sauder documented in US law schools under these same rankings ([Patterns §1](/concepts/patterns-and-failure-modes/)).

**Charity overhead ratios.** For years donors judged charities by the share of spending on administration and fundraising, and evaluators published the ratio. In 2013 the heads of GuideStar, Charity Navigator and the BBB Wise Giving Alliance wrote to donors that overhead "is a poor measure of a charity's performance" and that "many charities should spend more on overhead" ([open letter](https://nonprofitquarterly.org/2013/06/17/the-overhead-myth/)). Here the evaluators themselves retracted a cheap metric after it had shaped what charities did.

**GiveWell's mistakes page.** The counter-example is an evaluator that made admitting error part of its product. GiveWell keeps a public log of [its mistakes](https://www.givewell.org/about/our-mistakes) in research, grantmaking and operations. It publishes about itself the kind of candid negative assessment it asks of others.

**Internal prediction markets.** A 2021 report on why companies rarely adopt internal prediction markets ([Sempere, Yagudin & Lifland](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/dQhjwHA7LhfE8YpYF)) lists social disruptiveness among the likely reasons, alongside poor tooling and the difficulty of writing good questions. A market that surfaces bad news about a team is unwelcome to the people it exposes. This is the candidness problem inside one organization.

Capture is a different failure from backlash and is covered under [institutional design variables](/concepts/the-systems-view/#technical-and-institutional-design-variables): the World Bank's *Doing Business* index was discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities in two editions ([World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/statement/2021/09/16/world-bank-group-to-discontinue-doing-business-report)).

## What the cases suggest

- **Compression draws the fire.** Ofsted's detailed findings were not what was abolished; the single word was, as the overhead ratio was the part of charity rating its publishers disowned. Two cases suggest, without establishing, that the coarser and more consequential the published output, the stronger the pushback. That is a direct cost of the cheap, standardized outputs this wiki otherwise favours ([lesson 5 of the catalogue](/concepts/evaluation-systems-in-the-wild/)).
- **Exit is available when the evaluated supply the inputs.** A system that depends on the cooperation of those it rates can be boycotted. One that gathers its own data (product testers that buy their own units) cannot, which is part of why [funding and data independence](/concepts/the-systems-view/#technical-and-institutional-design-variables) matter.
- **A metric that steers behaviour badly will eventually be disowned**, sometimes by its own publishers. Robustness under optimization is a legitimacy property as well as an accuracy property.
- **Candidness is easier to demand of others than to practise.** Public error logs are rare. An evaluator that wants candid inputs has a stronger case if it is candid about itself.

## The candidness problem

The 2021–22 notes stated the general mechanism with a hypothetical: under certificates of impact, an organization watched by funders would issue certificates only for its best work, because a mediocre rating had become a liability. Once an evaluation matters to the evaluated, their incentive to be open with the evaluator falls. The internal-markets case is an observed instance. LLM evaluators do not remove this; they make it cheaper to produce the unwelcome assessment and so may bring the pushback sooner ([LLMs as Evaluators](/concepts/llm-evaluators/#what-llms-do-not-fix)).

## Rollout

The notes' thought experiment: an agency that published decent estimates of the impact of every politician, bill and organization would attract lawsuits and political pressure and might be shut down or captured before it stabilized. Their proposed answer, untested, is sequencing: start with private or commissioned evaluations at low stakes, publish more as norms and track records develop, and test in small willing communities first.

Law now constrains the end state. In the EU, AI systems used to evaluate learning outcomes, job candidates or creditworthiness are classed as high-risk ([AI Act Annex III](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/annex/3/)); the Digital Omnibus on AI, in force since July 2026, moved the start of those obligations to 2 December 2027 ([OJ L 2026/1744](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202601744)). Separately, the GDPR gives people a right not to be subject to decisions with legal or similarly significant effects based solely on automated processing ([Art. 22](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-22-gdpr/)), and the EU's top court has held that computing a score is such a decision when the party that acts on it draws strongly on the score ([CJEU, *SCHUFA*, C-634/21, 2023](https://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=C-634/21)). A nominal human sign-off on a model's verdict is therefore weak protection. A high-throughput evaluator of people needs a human whose judgment can change the outcome, and an appeal route, which are the institutional variables again.

The sibling RRP wiki's material on [identity and track records](https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org/environment/identity-and-track-records/) covers the related question of how evaluators earn trust over time.

# Reference
